ACCY111.title: Accounting Fundamentals In Society
ACCY111.description: This subject introduces the role of accounting information in society including its social and ethical aspects relating to both the individual and the organisation. The subject introduces basic accounting language, concepts and techniques to identify, classify, process, record and present accounting and financial information. The subject also considers accounting information that can be used for making decisions about past and future economic events in a variety of business and social settings.

ACCY121.title: Accounting for Decision Making
ACCY121.description: This subject introduces students to the role and use of accounting information in a variety of organisations and society. Students evaluate both financial and non-financial reports and their impact on accountability, decision-making and corporate governance. The subject introduces students to various analytical techniques in order to make sound decisions in a variety of business and social settings.

ACCY122.title: Accounting Principles
ACCY122.description: This subject introduces students to the principles of a double-entry accounting system to identify, classify, process, record and present accounting information. Students use accounting software to record business transactions, process accounting information and prepare financial statements. The subject introduces the role of ethics and professional judgement, in the context of an evolving business environment.

ACCY200.title: Financial Accounting
ACCY200.description: ACCY200 builds on the knowledge and skills students have acquired in both ACCY121 and ACCY122. In this subject, students will apply accounting standards and the conceptual framework to prepare and analyse general-purpose financial reports and related disclosures. This subject also develops the skills of professional judgement required to evaluate accounting practice in the changing legal and economic environment
prerequisites: ACCY111 and ACCY112 ORACCY121 and ACCY122 ORACCY111 and ACCY121 ORACCY112 and ACCY122

rules.description: ACCY111 and ACCY112 ORACCY121 and ACCY122 ORACCY111 and ACCY121 ORACCY112 and ACCY122

ACCY201.title: Advanced Financial Accounting
ACCY201.description: This subject builds on ACCY200 to understand and evaluate advanced accounting techniques. Students will apply critical and analytical skills to the interpretation and application of accounting standards in complex business arrangements. In this, subject students will have the opportunity to acquire the skills necessary for professional practice, including industry-based experience.

ACCY211.title: Management Accounting
ACCY211.description: The subject develops an understanding of the use of management accounting information for product costing, planning and control and decision-making. Students will apply a variety of quantitative tools and techniques to communicate relevant information to management. In this subject, students will apply ICT to analyse data and evaluate information for the preparation of management reports.
prerequisites: ACCY111 AND ACCY112 OR ACCY121 AND ACCY122 OR ACCY112 AND ACCY122 OR ACCY111 AND ACCY121

rules.description: ACCY111 AND ACCY112 OR ACCY121 AND ACCY122 OR ACCY112 AND ACCY122 OR ACCY111 AND ACCY121

ACCY228.title: Taxation: Law, Policy and Practice
ACCY228.description: This subject provides an overview of the Australian taxation system as it applies to individuals and business entities. Students examine income tax obligations, capital gains events, tax-effective structures, superannuation, and redundancy payments. The subject develops students' ability to identify and apply strategies for managing income and other taxes, equipping them with practical advisory skills relevant across accounting, business, and professional practice. Contemporary tax topics are introduced with reference to current ATO priorities, legislative developments, and real-world client scenarios.

ACCY231.title: Information Systems in Accounting
ACCY231.description: This subject introduces the students to accounting information systems and core business processes in an e-business environment. The subject addresses essential issues relating to information systems, such as the organisation, management and reporting of financial and non-financial data and information, and the internal control systems required to deal with risks, especially in core transaction cycles. The subject develops a critical understanding of the impact of new technology in transforming the value chain of business processes in relation to accounting, and the role of accountants in contemporary enterprise systems.
prerequisites: ACCY111 AND ACCY112 OR ACCY121 AND ACCY122 OR ACCY112 AND ACCY122 OR ACCY111 AND ACCY121

rules.description: ACCY111 AND ACCY112 OR ACCY121 AND ACCY122 OR ACCY112 AND ACCY122 OR ACCY111 AND ACCY121

ACCY244.title: Sustainability Accounting
ACCY244.description: This subject explores accounting for sustainability and accountability for social and environmental impacts across a range of organisations. It critically evaluates the current methods of sustainability accounting with respect to an ever-changing business and political landscape. This includes reporting and governance arrangements related to an organisation’s social and environmental impacts such as accounting for carbon and water, climate change, social responsibility, and modern slavery. Students will become equipped with the tools to critique and make decisions regarding business performance within a sustainability context.

ACCY305.title: Accounting and Professional Practice
ACCY305.description: In this subject, students will consolidate and integrate disciplinary knowledge to prepare for professional practice. This capstone experience will require students to critically evaluate current global developments in accounting, evaluate risks and opportunities and apply theory to explain accounting in its broader socio-political context.

ACCY312.title: Advanced Management Accounting
ACCY312.description: This subject provides an understanding of advanced management accounting techniques, in particular how they support organisational strategy, performance, management control and decision making processes. Students will develop skills to evaluate and communicate relevant information to a range of organisational stakeholders.

ACCY328.title: International Taxation
ACCY328.description: This subject covers cross border transactions with respect to the taxes the entity may incur as they trade and how these have an impact on the pricing of products. International taxation as it applies to the individual and a company are explored as well as its impact on their income and other trading activities. This subject also takes a comparative perspective of a number of issues confronting both companies and individuals who transact across national borders. Comparisons of taxation between countries such as Australia, UAE, UK and the USA will be examined.

ACCY342.title: Auditing and Assurance
ACCY342.description: This subject examines the nature and purpose of audit and assurance of general purpose financial reports and the regulatory and professional environment in which it operates. Topics include planning and risk assessment, the collection and evaluation of audit evidence and communication of a professional audit opinion.

ACCY801.title: Accounting and Financial Management
ACCY801.description: In this subject, students are provided with the foundations of accounting and financial management practices. Students will learn various analytical methods and techniques to evaluate both financial and non-financial information for effective decision-making in different organisational settings. No previous accounting knowledge or experience is assumed.

ACCY902.title: Financial Accounting
ACCY902.description: On completion of the subject, students will understand the role of professional judgment and be able to apply International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) to a range of contexts and business transactions and events. Students will develop the skills to evaluate the appropriateness of different regulatory requirements in the preparation of financial and non-financial reports and related disclosures.

AENG200.title: History of Architectural Design
AENG200.description: This subject will introduce the historical context and practice of architectural design, including an understanding of the relationship between engineers and architects. The subject will enable students to explore the differing conceptualisation of design between the disciplines of architecture and engineering. Students will gain foundational knowledge, skills and understanding in the history of architecture and engineering. These will be developed through the study of how construction and design have developed over time and in relation to their social, cultural and technological contexts. Students will take part in site visits to culturally and historically significant sites and iconic buildings in support of the subject learning. Within History of Architectural Design, students will be introduced to aboriginal heritage and knowledges as part of the curriculum. The subject will introduce and develop the skill of architectural communication through sketching. The practice of persuasive writing will be introduced and developed within this subject.

ARCH301.title: Archaeology in Action: Understanding the Archaeological record
ARCH301.description: This subject provides a practical and real-world approach to doing archaeology in an Australian context. It includes instruction on the steps required to gain permission from private, government and indigenous stakeholders to conduct investigations into Aboriginal cultural heritage in NSW. It provides practical experience in the use and application of a range of fundamental field, spatial and computational techniques to survey, record and interpret Aboriginal objects and the landscapes in which they are found. The subject also provides insights into the practicalities of compiling an Australian Heritage Impact Plan (AHIP) and the reporting of findings to relevant stakeholders. This subject is taught in weekly 3-hour workshops and four day excursions/fieldwork.
prerequisites: 12 credit points of 100 level and 12 credit points of 200 or 300 level subjects

rules.description: 12 credit points of 100 level and 12 credit points of 200 or 300 level subjects

ARCH302.title: Digging Down Under: Archaeology of Australasia
ARCH302.description: This subject introduces the archaeology of the Australasian region. It traces the history of human occupation in areas of Australia and its immediate neighbours through a range of key archaeological questions, such as the timing and nature of human arrival, megafauna extinctions, technology and economy, and explanations for cultural change. Through covering these issues, this subject illustrates the variability and complexity of human culture in Australasia, and also considers the influence of archaeological knowledge on modern ideas and representation of this region and its people.
prerequisites: 12 credit points of 100 level and 12 credit points of 200 or 300 level subjects

rules.description: 12 credit points of 100 level and 12 credit points of 200 or 300 level subjects

ARCH303.title: Dung, Death and Decay: Modern Scientific Methods in Archaeology
ARCH303.description: Students will be exposed to the methods and applications of four key components of archaeological science: geoarchaeology, geochronology, geochemistry and bioarchaeology. Students will learn how to use modern scientific methods to assess how archaeological deposits formed and may have changed over time; when archaeological objects were made and other events of interest took place; what kinds of environments/climates these people inhabited.

ARCH901.title: Archaeology in Action: Understanding the Archaeological record
ARCH901.description: This subject provides a practical and real-world approach to doing archaeology in an Australian context. It includes instruction on the steps required to gain permission from private, government and indigenous stakeholders to conduct investigations into Aboriginal cultural heritage in NSW. It provides practical experience in the use and application of a range of fundamental field, spatial and computational techniques to survey, record and interpret Aboriginal objects and the landscapes in which they are found. The subject also provides insights into the practicalities of compiling an Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Assessment report and the reporting of findings to relevant stakeholders. This subject is taught in weekly 3-hour workshops and three full-day excursions/fieldwork.
degree_restrictions: Not to count if having completed ARCH301 in an Undergraduate degree

ASSH003.title: Introduction to Visual Arts
ASSH003.description: ASSH003 is a studio based Visual Arts masterclass designed to support a student's creative practice and support them to further develop their HSC major work. The subject is designed around a series of intensive and dynamic studio workshops taught by professional practicing artists to support the development of studio projects. The aim of the subject is to enable the development of the student’s creative practice through both skill and concept development, material experimentation and through individual mentoring sessions with the lecturer. The studios offered will vary depending on the lecturers’ field of expertise and their availability however examples of the workshops taught could include drawing, painting, video & photography. A selection of the completed project work will be exhibited in the TAEM gallery at the end of the program.

ASSH005.title: Intro English: Critical Skills for Literature and Screen
ASSH005.description: Through examining a mix of written and filmic texts, this subject will provide students with a range of critical approaches to engage with texts, their meaning and their ethical and cultural implications. The class will touch on topics such as genre, post-colonialism, gender and sexuality, identity, class and ethnicity. It will also reinforce the skills and conventions attached to presenting clear, critically engaged, and supported arguments.

ASSH902.title: The Researcher: People, Places, Methods
ASSH902.description: What does it mean to be a 'researcher'? How does the researcher produce data, information and facts in a way that is trustworthy and persuasive? This subject takes students through key aspects of becoming a researcher and producing high‐quality, well informed and effective research. The subject investigates the different types of research methods available to researchers in the Humanities and Social Sciences: for example, interviews, archives, ethnographies, focus groups, participant observation, statistics and surveys. It will familiarise students with a variety of research techniques, protocols and ethics, and provide hands‐on experience with different research methods as well as highlighting the connection between academic research and the wider community.

ASSH903.title: The Project and the Plan
ASSH903.description: This subject offers a combination of coursework and in-class training in project management and thesis planning, as well as the opportunity to complete a preliminary research project undertaken for the MRes. The purpose of the subject is to ensure candidiates will have advanced knowledge and skills for professional work or future learning. The project is undertaken under the supervision of a supervior, and will contain elements such as (for example) a literature review or scoping for a major research project to be undertaken in the 2nd year of the MRes.

AUST101.title: Australian Studies: Histories, Cultures and Identities
AUST101.description: This subject revolves around an examination of Australian national identity, and thus on fundamental issues of belonging and inclusion. Taking a historical and cultural perspective, it asks what being Australian has meant to different people at different times. The subject explores the historical origins and foundations of national identity, how it has been contested and changed over time, and how historical, social, and cultural forces shape contemporary understandings and experiences of 'being Australian'. We consider social groups and individuals who have shaped dominant notions of national identity, as well as those who have challenged them. What does being Australian mean, for example, to Indigenous people, to women, to immigrants? And how have those meanings changed over time? We will particularly examine expressions of Australian national identity through some of its key practices and rituals - such as Australia Day, Anzac Day, sport, and the beach

AUST201.title: Eating Australia: A History of the Nation Through Food
AUST201.description:
“You are what you eat”—or so the saying goes. Eating certain foods and consuming particular drinks is not just a matter of survival, but a reflection of identity, culture, and history. This subject uses food and drink as a lens through which to critically examine Australian history and culture, with a particular focus on national identity.
Students will explore Australia’s Indigenous foodways, the impact of British colonialism, and the influence of multiculturalism on eating and drinking traditions. The subject also considers contemporary issues such as food security, globalisation, and the future of food. Histories of consumption reveal much about societies of the past and present. Today, iconic Australian foods include not only meat pies and pavlova but also kangaroo burgers and halal snack packs. While rum and beer dominated colonial drinking culture, wine is now the most widely consumed alcoholic beverage. How and why did these changes occur?
Through AUST201, students will develop skills in independent research and communicating historical insights to diverse audiences, while gaining a deeper understanding of how food shapes—and is shaped by —Australian society.

BALA201.title: Introduction to Business Analytics
BALA201.description: With growing quantities of data available, specific knowledge and skills are required in analysing this data to make evidence based decisions to enable organisations to achieve their strategic goals. This subject introduces students to the study of business analytics and provides the necessary foundations and skills to successfully complete the Business Analytics major. This subject introduces theoretical models and quantitative techniques and approaches to enable the analysis of large volumes of data for the purposes of decision making. The subject also introduces students to a variety of software tools relevant to the analysis and presentation of quantitative data.

BALA202.title: Big Data and Visual Analytics for Business
BALA202.description: This subject further investigates different categories of big data in business and the use of visual analytics techniques to study and analyse big data related to business activities of business organisations. The goal is to derive and translate hidden information in the big data into useful business information that can help to improve various aspects of a business. Students develop their knowledge and skills of data visualisation techniques through the use of appropriate tool and software. Different business problems are used throughout the course to illustrate different aspects of big data visual analytics. Understanding and interpreting these visual analytics outcomes is the focus of this course.

BALA301.title: Emerging Techniques and Tools in Business Analytics
BALA301.description: This subject explores emerging techniques and tools in business analytics. Concepts of predictive analytics and prescriptive analytics are introduced to students. Data mining and different techniques used in machine learning are also introduced and used to explore a range of business analytics scenarios for different business problems. Students explore and assess these emerging techniques and tools in business analytics to learn the effectiveness and applicability of these techniques and tools in various business problems related to current business environments.

BALA302.title: Business Analytics Industry Project
BALA302.description: This subject is the capstone subject within the Business Analytics major. The subject provides an opportunity for students to integrate knowledge and skills gained in previous subjects in the major through an industry-based group project. Working in groups, students will apply their knowledge and skills of business analytics to solve a ‘real life’ industry problem. Students will not only have to demonstrate the technical skills to solve the industry problem and justify their recommendations but also consider the ethics, and social responsibility aspects of their recommendations. The subject involves lectures, workshops and discussions where students are initially briefed on a ‘clients’ specific information-based problem and are then required to develop an analytical solution involving making recommendations to the client. The emphasis in the solution is around the analytical process including identifying information needs, acquiring the necessary information, interpreting it and using it as the basis for a set of strategic recommendations.

BCM110.title: Introduction to Communication and Media
BCM110.description: This foundation subject introduces students to ways of understanding media and communication practices, institutions and technologies. The subject takes an interdisciplinary approach to understanding how producers and consumers interact in a media saturated world. The subject will begin with the ways in which the media has been discussed in theory and in practice, and go on to examine how our communication practices and adoption and use of different technologies are integrated with our professional, social and political lives.

BCM112.title: Emergent Media
BCM112.description: This subject introduces you to the process of media convergence, emphasising the way in which digital media-driven technological change is accompanied by changes in the way we work, socialise and communicate. We focus on the emergent media dynamics of this process, and their effects on audiences, media platforms, and industries. You will establish and start developing an online presence across a range of platforms, and begin work on your first digital artefact.

BCM113.title: Media Ethics and Law
BCM113.description: Working in the communication and media industries requires a sound understanding of the legal framework within which you operate. But it is not just the law that we need to be aware of. There is also an ethical dimension that can manifest itself when we are considering the language we employ to talk about people with disabilities as well as particular racial, ethnic or religious groups, or other groups within society. Ethical issues arise whenever we choose photographs or video images to splice into our stories or even private conversations. As professional communicators we need to be aware of the damage that a wrong or misguided decision can have on a person’s reputation or emotional well-being. This subject will equip you with the tools required to address these and other questions you may confront while working in a position that involves communicating with people.

BCM115.title: Introduction to Screen Media
BCM115.description: This subject introduces students to screen media production by exploring the history and defining features of contemporary global cinema. Students develop foundational skills in key elements of screen media production including composition, lighting, camera techniques, audio, editing and post-production. The subject combines critical discussions with practical experiments focusing on the inventiveness of cinematic language as an expressive aesthetic form.

BCM116.title: Introduction to Immersive Media
BCM116.description: This subject introduces students to a range of screen media technologies employed to to create an immersive experience for the audience. The subject traces the historical and technological development from pre-cinema inventions to contemporary immersive experiences and explore the use of immersive media in artistic expression, scientific research, education, and entertainment. Students will develop foundational skills in key production technologies including animation techniques, camera 360º, augmented reality, virtual reality, and multiscreen projection. The subject combines critical discussions with practical experiments focusing on the inventiveness of immersive screen media.

BCM206.title: Future Networks
BCM206.description: The internet has revolutionised every aspect of our lives, reformatting and transcending personal, social and geographic boundaries. In this subject, we examine the emergence of global information networks and the rise of the network society. We explore the characteristics of the network society paradigm and the emerging phenomena of cyberculture, the attention economy, algorithmic feudalism, meme warfare, cyberwarfare, the internet of things, blockchains and decentralised finance. The assessments enable you to develop your own digital media projects or continue existing ones. All lectures and study materials are available online, and class interactions are structured as weekly seminars in which you prototype project ideas, workshop issues, and present your progress.
prerequisites: BCM 112 or BCM 114 or 36cp at any level

rules.description: BCM 112 or BCM 114 or 36cp at any level

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem A-On-Campus

BCM212.title: Understanding Research Practice
BCM212.description: If you are developing a product, designing a service or crafting a communication plan, you will need to think about how users or audiences will respond. This subject introduces you to the methods and challenges involved in researching lived experience, including your own. We look at user experience (UX) research, participatory co-design, creative and collaborative ethnography, and research as storytelling, in the context of traditional methods: surveying, interviews, focus groups. The subject emphasises ethical knowledge making, participant engagement and public communication. Students learn about these by designing, managing and reporting on a small experience-centred research project.

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem A-On-Campus

BCM214.title: Digital and Social Innovation
BCM214.description: This subject explores some of the major debates and the local and global impacts of digital and social innovation and digital disruption across the creative industries. Topics focus on a range of competing developments in virtual communities, blockchain applications, automation and robotics and the Internet of Things, for example, as well as the startups, innovation hubs, incubators, accelerators, co-working spaces and smart-city precincts where these activities are occurring. By investigating the interactive networks of people, public and private enterprises, industry events, technologies, regulation and governance, you will gain a deeper understanding of the entrepreneurial forces that are shaping the future of the digital economy.

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem B-On-Campus

BCM215.title: Game Media Industries
BCM215.description: Digital video games have emerged as one of the largest creative industries and most popular forms of media entertainment driving the global economy. This subject is designed for those unfamiliar with games while providing a challenge to established gamers as you develop skills in researching and analysing all forms of games media. We will explore the history and prehistory of video games through media archaeology and examine new trends in game media's participatory cultures, including different forms of fandom, live streaming and esports. In developing your digital artefacts and media projects, you will assemble an analytical framework to provide a publicly accessible critical analysis of game text or paratext. Your individual or collaborative approach might focus on PC gaming, consoles or mobile apps, explore issues in branding and merchandising or analyse new forms of online criticism and review. All lectures and materials for this subject are online, and the weekly seminars will provide the time and space to develop your project pitch, receive feedback and iterate your media project.

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem B-On-Campus

BCM216.title: Transmedia Storytelling
BCM216.description: Cultures, places, and lives are built from stories. Stories activate our imagination and help us understand lived experience beyond our own. Digital communication technologies are rapidly evolving the ways in which stories are told and shared. This subject introduces students to the fundamentals of transmedia storytelling. By engaging with different modes of storytelling in historical and contemporary practices, students develop practical skills including storyworld development, transmedia design, pitching, and collaborative media production.

BCM217.title: Documentary
BCM217.description: Documentary is one of the most exciting growth areas in contemporary cinema. This subject introduces key traditions and innovative forms of documentary film making from across the world. We focus on documentaries that address social justice issues and explore different ways of making an important issue compelling to audiences. The subject expands on production skills including how to pitch a project, how to write documentary treatments, and working with human subjects on camera

BCM222.title: Global Media and Social Justice
BCM222.description: Our ideas of who we are and what we are capable of are shaped by a variety of media and the stories they tell about gender, class and other dimensions of identity. In this subject we explore those stories, looking at where and how they are constructed, how they change over time and whose interests they serve. Our exploration of media will range across well-known forms (e.g. music, television, social media) as well as less obvious examples that mediate identity (e.g. maps, objects, bodies). The communication skills we develop in this subject include writing, presenting and thinking critically. This subject helps prepare you for the joy and challenge of the variety of identities you will encounter and inhabit at work and in life.

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem A-On-Campus

BCM300.title: Game Experience Design
BCM300.description: Understanding how to design experiences for others involves developing expertise in a complex set of specialist media and communication skills. The subject does not rely on previous experience with games and will introduce you to the global niche creative industry of board games and tabletop game experiences. You will learn how to ideate, pitch, prototype and negotiate feedback through playtesting and iteration to create unique analogue game experiences. All lectures for this subject are online and will support your learning about games and play, and the analysis of game mechanics, emergent narratives and story worlds. Although a physical product, analogue games are deeply reliant on internet cultures for their current success. You will develop knowledge in online crowdfunding and the challenges involved in the production, distribution, and advertising of physical entertainment media products. All workshops are run in the Creative Industries Maker Studio where you will work independently and collaboratively to create digital media projects and analogue game experiences for a range of players and public audiences.

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem C-On-Campus
UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem C-On-Campus

BCM303.title: Collaborative Production Workshop
BCM303.description: This subject explores the skills, strategies and professional expectations of collaborative media production. An examination of relevant principles, practices and industry case studies provides the basis for teams of students with different media production expertise to collaborate in the development of common projects.

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem C-On-Campus

BCM304.title: Advanced Screen Media Project
BCM304.description: This capstone subject enables students to further their screen media production skills developed in the major. Students are guided in reflecting their learning outcomes, identifying future goals, and finding a pathway into the creative industries.  The final outcomes are presented in a public graduate screening.

BCM320.title: Digital Asia
BCM320.description: This subject explores a range of contemporary Asian digital media cultures and communication practices, and examines the significance of Digital Asia in a global context. It provides students with opportunities to investigate and critically reflect upon the production and consumption of new cultural forms and cutting-edge developments, as for example, in mobile applications and online platforms, fan cultures, K-pop and J-Pop phenomena, social media, microblogging, digital games and e-commerce; as well as immersive Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality genres and experiences. Through lectures and tasks exploring these topics, including the impacts of networked activism across the region, students will learn to locate Digital Asia within specific historical, cultural, industrial and diasporic contexts and perspectives.

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem B-On-Campus

BCM325.title: Future Cultures
BCM325.description: The ancient arts of divination are symbolic of a deeply human need to anticipate and plan for the future. In this subject, you will learn contemporary approaches to futurology through futures studies and the production of a digital artefact that addresses the future in the short, medium, and long term. You will examine the tensions between the representation and the realities of future cultures through the live analysis of landmark science fiction films. Your independent projects will respond to the issues raised by the presence and use of computers, networks and artificial intelligence in all aspects of contemporary social life, including communication, health, employment, education, art, entertainment, industry, and the environment.

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem B-On-Campus

BCM331.title: Australian Content, Global Context
BCM331.description: In this subject, we examine the production and protection of Australian screen content in the global market. We analyse audience demand both in Australia and in foreign markets for media content, and then look at the policies and funding strategies that protect local content producers in these markets. Students collaborate to design and implement audience-centred research projects focused on creative and achievable recommendations for promoting cultural and creative diversity in Australia, in the context of the global media trade

BCM333.title: Hollywood and Beyond
BCM333.description: This subject explores innovative and exciting examples of filmmaking from around the world. Focusing on genre, we look at the migration of film genres from Hollywood to Europe and Asia and the influence of other industries on Hollywood. The subject focuses on key genres that may include crime, comedy, melodrama and science fiction, showing how such genres change over time and are informed by the cultures that make them. For the final project you will collaborate to create the program for a mini film festival on a genre of your choice, selecting and researching the films and designing the marketing, venue and activities.

BCM389.title: Career Readiness: from Student to Professional
BCM389.description: Careers in media, humanities, and creative arts are diverse. In this subject, you will develop knowledge, skills and confidence to navigate the transition from university to professional careers. Through reflection and exploring varied career journeys, you will critically consider ideas about work, career, professionalism, the future world of work. You will also engage in career research and critical reflection to develop personally relevant strategies to navigate your career in the changing world of work. This subject centres practical communication, enabling you to articulate your capabilities, professional identity, and aspirations in industry relevant formats to transition from university to professional careers in the media, humanities and creative arts.

BIOL103.title: Molecules, Cells and Organisms
BIOL103.description:
BIOL103 is the study of molecules, cell and organisms fundamental to biology. This subject provides an introduction to the topic areas of cell biology, biochemistry, biotechnology, genetics, microbiology and immunology. Students will look closely at the links between structure and function in cells and important biological molecules whilst investigating cellular division and mechanisms to control the cell cycle and prevent cancer. You will hear about techniques in genetic engineering and break throughs in biotechnology. You will learn about different microorganisms and their role in human, animal and/or plant health and explore the physiology of the immune system. Students will also learn from Indigenous stories to develop cultural and scientific understanding. In addition, students will utilise frameworks, such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UNSDGs), to develop creative solutions to some of our world's biggest challenges.  Through engagement in these group research projects you will develop skills in effective research, problem-solving and communication; alongside teamwork, self reflection and peer assessment whilst developing your digital literacy skills in presenting your research through multiple formats (videos, pamphlets, podcasts, infographics etc). Through generation of an electronic Portfolio you can showcase your skill development.
 
This subject is related to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Find out more: www.uow.edu.au/united-nations-sustainable-development-goals/sdg-subjects-and-courses/

BIOL104.title: Evolution, Biodiversity and Environment
BIOL104.description:
This subject aims to provide students with a comprehensive introduction to whole organism biology, from species to populations, communities and ecosystems. Specifically, the subject explores the identity, anatomical and life-history characteristics of the main groups of organisms, their patterns of diversity across Earth, the processes of evolution and speciation, ecology and conservation biology. In addition, through a series of practical classes, the subject equips students with an understanding of the scientific process, ways in which experiments are designed and implemented, the processes of data collection and analysis and hypothesis testing.
 
This subject is related to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Find out more: www.uow.edu.au/united-nations-sustainable-development-goals/sdg-subjects-and-courses/

BIOL105.title: Functional Biology of Animals and Plants
BIOL105.description: This subject explores how the structure and function of animals and plants solves the puzzle of survival in a wide range of environments. To achieve this, physiological processes work together from cells, to organ systems. The curriculum covers body plans, systems for sensing and responding to the environment, mechanisms to acquire energy and nutrients for growth and reproduction in both plants and animals. Additionally, parasitic relationships in plants and animals, and the fundamentals of animal behaviour are covered. This course includes animal dissections. While direct participation is not mandatory, all students will be assessed on the material covered

BIOL213.title: Principles of Biochemistry
BIOL213.description: BIOL213 focuses on the principles of biochemistry. With increasingly robust technologies that provide detailed views of molecular processes, progress in biochemistry is exciting - providing new wonders and new challenges. Students will explore the biochemical structure and biological function of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids and their subunits. Students will learn about enzymes as important reaction catalysts of biological systems, without which life would not exist.  Through an exploration of information pathways students will learn about the molecular structure of genetic material, how this genetic information is transmitted from one generation to the next with high fidelity and how this genetic information is ultimately expressed in the astonishing variety of protein molecules in a living cell. Through the exploration of real-life case studies students will gain an appreciation of how biochemistry continues to solve modern challenges in human and environmental health but also plays a role in sustainability, food security, water and sanitation, just to name a few. Thus touching on the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.  Through engagement in group and individual activities, students will develop skills in effective problem-solving and communication, alongside teamwork, whilst developing digital literacy and data integrity skills through utilisation of an electronic laboratory notebook. Providing students with professional skills sought after by employers.
prerequisites: BIOL103 and CHEM101 and CHEM102 or CHEM104 and CHEM105

rules.description: BIOL103 and CHEM101 and CHEM102 or CHEM104 and CHEM105

BIOL214.title: The Biochemistry of Energy and Metabolism
BIOL214.description: BIOL214 focuses on metabolic processes, essential to all forms of life. With an emphasis on, but not limited to, human health and disease, students will discover the central role of biochemical pathways in the degradation and synthesis of carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids, and the relevance of energy carriers, enzymes, and vitamins to these processes. By studying photosynthesis, students will explore the importance of sunlight in sustaining life. While acquiring real-life laboratory and data skills, practicals will reinforce understanding of metabolic processes and teach scientific processes of discovery and validation. Collectively, this subject aligns with United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UNSDGs) including "Life on Land" and "Good Health and Well-Being" and will contribute to professional skills sought after by employers in sectors relating to science, medicine and health.

BIOL215.title: Introductory Genetics
BIOL215.description: In BIOL215, a range of areas encompassed by genetics and genetic engineering are explored through lectures, student tutorial presentations and experimental practical classes. These include: A history of DNA as the genetic material; Analysis of DNA; Regulation of gene activity in prokaryotes; eukaryotes and bacteriophage; Mechanisms for the rearrangement and exchange of genetic material; Approaches for genetic engineering, including the cloning of DNA, screening of recombinants and the production of a recombinant protein.  The ethics of current and emerging genetic technologies will be considered and the big data generated by ever-improving sequencing technologies discussed. The current and controversial topics of gene editing, genome engineering, and whole genome sequencing will be the focus of the group presentation task which will importantly develop skills in research, and communication alongside peer assessment and self-reflection. Practical skills will be developed through a project that explores the concepts of cloning, sequence analysis and gene regulation, complementing much of the lecture material and providing an opportunity for you to advance your scientific research and writing skills. Both of these tasks foster team-work which is a key professional skill desired by majority of employers. You will capture this skill development in an electronic portfolio.

BIOL240.title: Biodiversity of Marine and Freshwater Organisms
BIOL240.description: Introduction to biodiversity in aquatic ecosystems; including algae, plants, invertebrates and vertebrates. Quantification and importance of biological diversity. Human impacts on natural systems and the loss of biodiversity. Making and curating a collection of selected groups of organisms. Please note that this subject may involve animal dissections. While direct participation is not mandatory, all students will be examined on the material.

BIOL241.title: Biodiversity of Terrestrial Organisms
BIOL241.description: The subject will cover the phylogeny, classification, morphology, and physiology of terrestrial organisms. It will investigate how the structure and function of organisms is influenced by, and interacts with, the terrestrial environment. Students will learn the principles of identification of both plants and animals and will develop and curate a collection of plants. Small local field trips focused on surveying for a range of taxa may occur.

BIOL251.title: Principles of Ecology
BIOL251.description: Factors and processes influencing the distribution, abundance and diversity of organisms. Population ecology: growth and regulation. Species interactions. Natural and anthropogenic disturbance. Community structure and dynamics in space and time. Sampling methods and techniques in ecology. Design and statistical analysis of sampling programs and experiments. Communicating science.

BIOL252.title: Evolution and Behaviour
BIOL252.description: Students will investigate the key concepts of evolutionary theory, selection, drift, mutation, gene expression and inheritance, plasticity and canalization, factors changing frequencies, mating systems, sexual selection, mate choice, sociality, life history strategies and trade-offs.

BIOL341.title: Immunity and Infection
BIOL341.description: This subject focuses on our current understanding of aspects of microbial pathogens, the immune system, and the ways in which the immune system defends the body against pathogens. The relationship between host and microbe is a delicate balancing act. We will learn about the major groups of microbial pathogens, and important aspects of clinical microbiology, before examining the multiple facets of the immune system in humans. The interactions between pathogens and the immune system will be explored, both in theory and as an integrated part of the practical exercises. We will discuss the impact of infectious disease on the global community, and the importance of harnessing beneficial microbes to enhance global health. We will explore the most recent advances in diagnostics and therapeutics including vaccine development and whole genome sequencing, to understand approaches to controlling infection. As such, this topic addresses issues central to the UN Sustainable Development Goals of Health and Well-being and Reduced Inequalities. We will build on your career-ready skills through exposure to industry relevant concepts, the development of written communication skills and team based laboratory work. You will gain experience in practical skills that explore critical techniques medical research and clinical microbiology.

BIOL343.title: Techniques in Biotechnology and Medical Research
BIOL343.description: This subject is all about the latest and greatest innovations in biotechnology and medical research.  In this subject you will learn about genes and genomes, the very blueprints of life at the core of biomedical data science and bioinformatics. We will investigate how gene and protein levels can be altered to promote our understanding of molecular pathways relevant to cell function, development and disease. We will look at the applications of biotechnology to produce vaccines, harness the power of viruses for human gene therapy and generate transgenic plants that could aid global access to food. As such, this topic addresses technologies at the interface of the UN Sustainable Development Goals of Zero Hunger and Good Health and Well-being. We will build on your career-ready skills in our tutorials that are designed to develop your presentation, communication and team-working skills. You will gain experience in practical skills that explore critical techniques in biotechnology and medical research.

BIOL362.title: Ecophysiology
BIOL362.description: Physiological and biochemical characterisation of organisms in relation to size, metabolic intensity, and response to environmental variables. Physiological responses of plants and animals to variations in light intensity, spectral quality, temperature, gas composition and pressure. Evolution of aerobic metabolism, aerobic capacity and endothermy. Physiological processes associated with phenotypic plasticity and adaptive traits. Physiological correlates of life-history variation. This subject may involve the use of animals, animal tissues or animal-derived products in order to achieve specific learning objectives.

BMEG202.title: Bioinstrumentation
BMEG202.description: This subject will introduce 1) engineering instrumentation related to measurement of biomedical signals (including EMG and ECG) and 2) the principles of sensing elements, sensors, and actuator technologies. It will cover the design methodology (including circuits, signal analysis and electrical safety) for biomedical instrumentation systems, involving an instrumentation design project. It will also cover the use of bio-instrument in areas such as orthotics, prosthetics, exoskeletons, and rehabilitation and medical robotics.

BMEG306.title: Biomaterials and Tissue Engineering
BMEG306.description: The principles of materials science and cell biology in the context of the design of medical implants, artificial organs, and matrices for tissue engineering, surface characterization of biomaterials and analysis of protein adsorption on biomaterials as well as molecular and cellular interactions with biomaterials, tissue and organ regeneration and tissue remodeling following implantation in various organs, design of implants and prostheses based on control of biomaterials-tissue interactions, and a comparative analysis of intact, biodegradable, and bio-replaceable implants with reference to case studies. Examples of engineering tissues for replacing cartilage, bone, tendons, ligaments, skin and liver will be presented.

BUS002.title: Responsible Business Decision-making
BUS002.description: This subject gives Year 12 students the tools to understand the fundamental interrelationships that exist in responsible business decision-making. It explores responsible decision-making with reference to the impact on company strategy, disciplinary functions, stakeholders and customers. Students are challenged to consider the greater impact on the environment and society. The HSC business studies syllabus will be referred to and extended.
degree_restrictions: Only Year 12 students registered for the Summer master class subject BUS 002 can enrol in this subject

BUS101.title: Principles of Responsible Business
BUS101.description: The subject explores responsible and ethical business in contemporary organizations as they relate to business practice and sustainable development. It provides students with theoretical and philosophical understandings of ethics to critically evaluate individual and organizational responses to sustainable development in organizational decision-making. The topics covered will include a focus on ethical and social responsibility in business. Key challenges addressed include the environment and climate change, human rights, bribery prevention and governance, sustainable development, globalization and technology. Students will examine these challenges in contemporary organisational contexts from a variety of theoretical and practical perspectives, and the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals.

BUS121.title: Statistics for Business
BUS121.description: The aim of the subject is to introduce students to quantitative techniques and their application to the business world with an emphasis on the decision-making process. The main focus of the subject is business statistics and topics will include descriptive statistics, probability, sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, elementary correlation, regression analysis and time series forecasting. Students are also introduced to the use of computer programs for estimation and analysis to improve business decision-making.

BUS200.title: Innovation for Global Goals
BUS200.description: This subject gives students the tools and frameworks to understand, create and action unique innovative ideas to super wicked problems using the globally-recognised United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Through the use of systems thinking principles, students will apply an interconnected approach to tackling societal, biosphere and economic global challenges. Students will have the opportunity to collaborate with University students from across UOW to brainstorm ideas, workshop ideas with industry professionals and pitch ideas to experts.

BUS302.title: International Study Tour in Business
BUS302.description:
This subject, delivered in person, involves an international travel component. In person pre-departure classes will take place on campus, ahead of an experiential international learning activity.
Students build on their academic knowledge and professional skills developed during their studies with an international experiential opportunity. The embedded work integrated learning subject prepares students for the future world of work by engaging them in purposefully designed work-based activities, cross-cultural communication and exposure to international industry, while providing opportunities for reflection and engaged feedback within assessments.
prerequisites: Students must have completed 48 credit points of study

rules.description: Students must have completed 48 credit points of study

BUS303.title: International Perspectives on Sustainable Business Practices
BUS303.description: This subject provides students with an international experiential learning opportunity to apply multidisciplinary knowledge in addressing sustainability challenges across diverse cultural and business contexts. Through a blend of pre-departure classes and an immersive study tour abroad, students will explore environmental, social, and economic aspects of sustainability. They will analyse sustainability challenges and opportunities within international practices, examining emerging sustainability technologies and fostering cross-cultural communication and ethical awareness. By engaging with international peers, industry professionals, and local communities, students will gain a deeper understanding of how sustainability challenges impact business practices and how cultural variations shape sustainability decisions.
degree_restrictions: Manual Enrolment by UOW staff

BUS330.title: Economics and Finance Applied Research Project
BUS330.description: The subject is designed to offer students an applied learning opportunity in the field of economics and finance. A variety of options will be offered which may include, for example, an international stock exchange field trip, workplace project or more traditional research project, in order to apply their discipline specific knowledge of economics and finance to a real world issue. Students will define the scope of the economics and finance issue or problem faced, identify the relevant theoretical framework and methodology to be utilised in its analysis, and report findings and recommendations. The intended goal is for students to draw upon key principles of economics and finance learnt through their course and apply this toward an issue of contemporary relevance.
degree_restrictions: Restricted to Bachelor of Economics and Finance students.

BUS344.title: Climate Change and Business Development
BUS344.description: This subject will introduce students to the changes that business need to manage in driving the transition towards net zero, focusing on sustainable business strategy, innovation and leadership. Students will be encouraged to explore the role that they play in combating climate change through building business models that are resilient and provide shared value in the net-zero, resource-efficient economy of the 21st century.

BUS391.title: Professional Experience in Business
BUS391.description: Professional Experience in Business enables students to apply the knowledge learned at university via work integrated learning and/or a real world focussed innovation project in an industry context and become work ready. To attain a place within the program, students competitively apply in the prior semester, and are selected for a domestic or international internship or to complete a proposed innovation project in their discipline areas. The application and recruitment process is part of the learning. The core purpose of the program is to offer experiential learning opportunities combined with rigorous reflection on value based responsible leadership and organisational practices and career alignment.
prerequisites: 72 credit points including BUS 101 + 65 WAM + demonstration of good reflective, critical analytical thinking and essay/ report writing skills.

rules.description: 72 credit points including BUS 101 + 65 WAM + demonstration of good reflective, critical analytical thinking and essay/ report writing skills.

BUS903.title: Professional Internship
BUS903.description: This subject empowers postgraduate students to synthesise and apply advanced knowledge and skills in their study area through an internship, preparing them for the professional demands of the industry. Working under the dual supervision of an organisational expert and an academic mentor, students will (1) execute a significant workplace project to integrate academic learning with practical professional application, (2) actively engage in diverse operational tasks within their internship organisation, demonstrating adaptability and skill in a professional environment, (3) develop a detailed portfolio that documents the range of work and projects completed during the internship, highlighting technical and non-technical competencies, (4) critically reflect on personal and professional development to evaluate the advanced skills and competencies acquired, and (5) undergo an assessment of collaborative, time management, communication and organisational abilities by their workplace supervisor and academic mentor.

BUS980.title: Business Research Proposal
BUS980.description: This subject is designed to provide business-based Higher Degree Research with substantial knowledge of research principles and methods applicable to their field of work or learning in order that they can plan and execute an original research design and research proposal. It provides discipline-independent cognitive and research skills in order to demonstrate expert theoretical knowledge, the ability to think critically, evaluate existing knowledge and ideas and undertake systematic investigation and reflection on current theory. The subject explores different research paradigms, and related methodologies, entails substantial searching, reviewing and critiquing of relevant literature, and examines a range of data collection methods and critical analysis. Finally, students are required to present cogently a complex investigation of original research in their final proposal.

BUS981.title: Business Research Proposal
BUS981.description: This subject is designed to provide business-based Higher Degree Research with substantial knowledge of research principles and methods applicable to their field of work or learning in order that they can plan and execute an original research design and research proposal. It provides discipline-independent cognitive and research skills in order to demonstrate expert theoretical knowledge, the ability to think critically, evaluate existing knowledge and ideas and undertake systematic investigation and reflection on current theory. The subject explores different research paradigms, and related methodologies, entails substantial searching, reviewing and critiquing of relevant literature, and examines a range of data collection methods and critical analysis. Finally, students are required to present cogently a complex investigation of original research in their final proposal.

BUS993.title: Applied Data Analysis
BUS993.description: This subject introduces students to the analysis of both qualitative and quantitative data in social science and business research. This will allow students to demonstrated knowledge in using and applying appropriate data analysis techniques. This subject will introduce students to quantitative techniques such as; multiple regression, logistic regression models, discriminate analysis and factor analysis. It will also introduce qualitative analysis including both manual and computer aided forms of data reduction, thematic analysis and coding. Students will develop and extend analytical skills required for application of those techniques in research, and interpretation of both quantitative and qualitative outputs.

BUS996.title: Introduction to Research and Research Methods
BUS996.description: In this subject, students will examine methodological issues in social science and business research, and then explore the foundations for choosing methods and techniques in business and social science research. This will allow students to demonstrate knowledge of the qualitative and quantitative methods for conducting research. Students will develop an understanding of the range of quantitative and qualitative methods; an appreciation of the ethical issues in business and social science research; and the skills to critically evaluate and apply appropriate methods.

BUS997.title: Literature Review
BUS997.description: This subject will give students the opportunity to conduct and receive feedback on a literature review focussed on the topic they plan to examine in their research. The Literature Review can be expected to form part of the first draft of the thesis. It is an evolving and substantial piece of work that will develop as the research focus and methodologies take shape.

CACS111.title: Introduction to Creative Practice
CACS111.description: What are you curious about? This subject invites you, as emerging creative practitioners, to discover how to make sense of the world, challenge assumptions, and drive cultural change and innovation.This subject introduces you to the foundation of creative practice-based learning and research. You will draw on historical and contemporary examples from creative writing, music, performance and theatre, and visual arts and design, to discover different ways of thinking and making.You will attend exhibitions and events, engage with creative professionals, and experiment with diverse approaches to creative inquiry. Through guided activities, you will ask questions, reflect critically on creative methods and processes, and begin to articulate your own voice and perspective.

CACS112.title: Creative Knowledges
CACS112.description: Creative Arts practice begins with respect and care for Country, for community, and for each other. This subject asks you to consider your place within the world: where you’re from and where you might be headed. It grounds your creative practice in care and connection – because creativity begins with listening and learning. Through on-Country experiences, storytelling, and sharing knowledge, you will learn about the place on which UOW is situated, underneath Geera (Mt Keira), a traditional site of learning, surrounded by Land, Sea, and Sky Country. You will explore the ways cultural knowledges shape all of us, acknowledge your responsibilities to place, and reflect on how a deep engagement with place strengthens creative practice.

CACS113.title: Communication for Creatives
CACS113.description: Creative artists need to be skilled communicators in order to connect with their audiences, build support for their creative endeavours, and advocate for the cultural, social, and economic value of their work. This subject develops your capacity to communicate clearly and confidently across a range of written, audiovisual and embodied modes, and to adapt your communication to different contexts, audiences, and platforms. In doing so, we focus on the interpersonal dimensions of creative practice: your ability to listen carefully, engage in meaningful conversation, and respond to others’ work with honesty, care, and critical attention – skills that are essential to both creative practice and professional life. The subject will guide you to reflect on your creative identity and professional aspirations, gaining a clearer sense of who you are as a practitioner and the communication skills you will need for your future careers.

CACS114.title: Creative Communities
CACS114.description: What does it mean to create value with, and for, communities through creative practice?In this subject, you will explore how creative practitioners collaborate across networks of people, places, and disciplines to real needs in the world. Through this, it asks you to consider the role of a creative practitioner – not only as a maker, but as a collaborator, a listener, and a contributor to communities beyond their own.Through case studies drawn from the broader arts and cultural landscape, you will examine the transformative value of interdisciplinary creative practice, reflect on what it means to create with and for communities, and consider the responsibilities that come with that work.Using this knowledge, and working to a real-world challenge brief, you will produce creative responses that generate new knowledge and tangible outcomes for a community. In doing so, you will discover what it means to make work that adds value to the world.

CACS300.title: Critical Thinking
CACS300.description: This subject examines key aspects of critical theory and its relevance to creative practices and industries. These ways of thinking offer models for generating and shaping creative works, while also challenging conventional understandings of the social, political and aesthetic value of creative production. Students will consider the implications of these theories across multiple disciplines: Creative Writing, Music, Theatre and Performance, and Visual Arts and Design.

CACW100.title: Introduction to Creative Writing
CACW100.description: This subject offers a practical introduction to creative writing through the three key genres of poetry, prose, and scriptwriting. It introduces students to a wide range of creative texts with the aim of developing their writing, editing, and critical skills. It provides students with the opportunity to workshop their writing in class and engage with the work of their peers on the way to producing three creative portfolios.

CACW107.title: How Words Work – Editing, Form and Style
CACW107.description: At its best, creative writing can be vibrant and life-changing: it can unsettle, celebrate, console, persuade, and entertain. This subject explores the foundations of writing, with a focus on how words function in a creative context. You will learn the principles of grammar, punctuation, and style, and identify their purpose in a range of texts: poetic, dramatic, and narrative. You will be introduced to the stages of editing creative work within a publishing context, including structural editing, copyediting, and proofreading. Through hands-on editorial practice and analysis of texts, you will learn to write precisely and capably, as well as gain the skills to respond to others’ writing respectfully and effectively.

CACW201.title: Poetry Studio
CACW201.description: This subject explores a range of verse forms. Students will gain the knowledge and skills necessary to write confidently in these verse forms, and will be introduced to the work of a wide variety of poets, both historical and contemporary. Imagery, metaphor, rhythm, rhyme and other poetic devices will be discussed in the context of the students’ own creative work. Students will hone their communication, editing and drafting skills in a workshop setting.

CACW202.title: Script Studio
CACW202.description: This subject immerses students in the techniques and theory of writing in dramatic form. Writing strategies for scriptwriting will be examined and a variety of dramatic forms will be explored. Craft skills such as characterisation, dialogue, mise-en-scène, storyworlds and dramaturgy will be discussed in the context of the students’ own creative work. Students will hone their communication, editing and drafting skills in a workshop setting.

CACW203.title: Prose Studio
CACW203.description: This subject examines the development of prose fiction writing in both microfiction and short forms. There will be an ongoing examination of writing strategies in a range of modes. An intensive workshopping of participants work will operate throughout the subject. Particular attention will be paid to structure, plot, character, time/place management, point of view, and the use of description and metaphor.
prerequisites: At least 6cp of CACW at 100 level

rules.description: At least 6cp of CACW at 100 level

CACW231.title: Writing, Representation and Power
CACW231.description: This subject explores the relationship between writing and ideology: the philosophical, cultural and political modes that affect creative production. In this subject, we will consider the implications of writing fiction in historical contexts as well as contemporary Australian society. Specifically, we will reflect on questions of textual power, exploring the relationship between ideology and textual structure, as well as the ways writers might resist textual control. We will also focus on questions of responsibility, investigating topics such as writers’ relationships with their culture, and the ethics of writing. We will explore these questions through two approaches: by analysing existing literary texts in the light of critical theory and by applying the ideas discussed to our own writing.

CACW303.title: Genre and Form
CACW303.description: This subject offers students an opportunity to focus on a specific and specialised genre/form of writing. The focus of the subject will vary each semester and may include: - Contemporary writing since 1980 and its themes - Genre Crime writing - Narrative and voice - Writing novels and novellas - The Short Story - Writing for children - Writing for the screen - Creative non fiction Students will be advised in advance of each semester which topic will be covered.

CACW304.title: Critical/ Creative Writing
CACW304.description: This subject examines the interactions between creative practice and critical ideas that provoke and extend the possibilities of writing. It provides writers with an opportunity to consider how we might use theories about writing to strengthen our practice and also to question the process and production of writing. In this subject we will analyse key critical ideas about writing, evaluate their efficacy, and reflect on the cultural and ethical implications of textual production. We will apply them to specific creative texts, including our own.

CACW307.title: The Professional Writer
CACW307.description: This subject introduces students to a range of professional writing styles, mediums, and opportunities. These may include book reviews, writing for TV/web series, op-eds, children’s books, podcasts, speechwriting, freelance editing, travel writing, and more. Students will draw from skills developed in first and second years to expand their practical repertoire with the aim of developing their professional capabilities and expanding their career prospects. Along the way, students will be introduced to specialist skills and knowledge critical to helping them find their way in the creative industries as successful, working writers.

CACW308.title: Writing, Representation and Power
CACW308.description: This subject explores the relationship between writing and power: the philosophical, cultural, and political modes that affect creative production. In this subject, we will consider the implications of writing fiction in historical contexts as well as contemporary Australian society. Specifically, we will reflect on questions of textual power, exploring the relationship between power and textual structure, as well as the ways writers might resist textual control. We will also focus on questions of responsibility, investigating topics such as writers’ relationships with their culture, and the ethics of writing. We will explore these questions through two approaches: by analysing existing literary texts in the light of critical theory; and by applying the ideas discussed to our own writing.

CACW310.title: Writing Our Future
CACW310.description: This subject examines writing strategies used in creative fiction and non-fiction texts that address issues crucial to climate change and the environmental humanities. Particular attention will be paid to voice, structure, time and place management, point of view, and the use of description and metaphor. New emerging forms and nomenclature (such as as cli-fi fiction, post-natural writing and eco-writing) will be examined. In addition, students will hone their communication, editing and drafting skills in a workshop setting.

CAMS101.title: Music Skills 1
CAMS101.description: This subject provides an introduction to music theory and practice through an integrated approach to aural, notation and vocal training. Individual practice of these skills outside class time is a requirement of this subject. Students gain experience in composition and performance through a series of creative exercises, including the presentation of a song.

CAMS102.title: Music Skills 2
CAMS102.description: Building on the foundations laid in Music 1, students continue their development of practical and theoretical skills with a special focus on ensemble music. Students learn how to arrange music for a group of musicians, as well as perform music collaboratively. They will also develop a critical vocabulary to discuss music and articulate their creative aims.

CAMS103.title: Introduction to Audio Production
CAMS103.description: This subject provides an introduction to audio recording, editing, and mixing techniques. Through a combination of critical listening, analysis and practical instruction, students gain a conceptual and practical understanding of basic acoustics, microphone theory, and digital audio production. Concepts of structure and arrangement are introduced and students apply conceptual and practical skills to the creation of sound and music works using digital audio workstations.

CAMS104.title: Introduction to Music Production
CAMS104.description: This subject provides an introduction to music production using desktop sampling and sequencing tools for studio and live performance contexts. Hardware and software interface concepts are explored along with an introduction to software synthesis. The different challenges and opportunities presented by live performance and studio production are identified and examined alongside a survey of approaches to the composition, arrangement and preparation of musical materials. Through a combination of critical analysis and practical work, the subject provides a broad introduction to music composition, arranging and production in digital audio workstation (DAW) environments.

CAMS201.title: Music Studio 1
CAMS201.description: This subject provides a workshop environment in which the knowledge acquired through previous theory and skills subjects is put into practice. Students are introduced to the core skills needed in 2nd year music studio through a series of guided composition and performance exercises that will build skills in harmony, notation, vocal and instrumental arrangement, as well as performance and improvisation. A range of musical styles is explored through technical and creative practice in a collaborative setting.

CAMS202.title: Music Studio 2
CAMS202.description: This is the second of two second year music studio subjects that builds on skills obtained through previous studio tasks to extend students technical and creative abilities with a particular focus on ensemble music. Working collaboratively in small groups, students explore a variety of contemporary compositional and performance techniques and approaches through practical workshops and rehearsals. Peer feedback forms an important part of the learning and development process, and issues concerning stage presentation and production are also considered. The subject culminates in the presentation of ensemble works in a public performance.

CAMS203.title: Recording Studio
CAMS203.description: This subject provides a detailed exploration of the audio recording studio as a creative and practical tool. Through a combination of technical instruction, theoretical analysis and critical listening, students gain a comprehensive understanding of modern recording studio concepts and processes. Students build on existing knowledge of acoustic, electronic and digital audio production to extend and develop their conceptual and practical skills through the creation of complex sound and music works in the recording studio environment.

CAMS204.title: Music and Culture
CAMS204.description: This subject explores a range of musical styles and genres from various cultures of the world, with a focus on traditional music and instruments in a post-colonial era. It examines the role of music in different societies and cultures, and examines themes such as: music and ritual, race and gender, transmission and appropriation, the influence of globalisation and the construction of identity through music.

CAMS232.title: Critical Studies in Music 2
CAMS232.description: This subject takes a non-linear approach to the key historical developments and theoretical debates that have shaped music today. It examines milestones and breakthroughs in the history of music from the introduction of notation and the development of harmony and counterpoint, to innovations in instrument building and the impact of music and recording technologies. The purpose is not only to provide an overview of the key periods, movements and artists in the history of western music, but also to reflect on their relevance and application to current music practice. Students also develop formal skills in music history, theory and criticism.

CAMS301.title: Music Studio 3
CAMS301.description: This subject immerses students in a range of skills essential to the self-producing musician. Building on experiences from previous creative projects, each student will develop a large-scale composition for ensemble with the possibility of collaborating with other student performers and/or incorporating digital media. Strong emphasis is placed on the development of an individual musical style as well as the ability to engage effectively in a coherent program of creative development through a process of technical, conceptual and creative enquiry. To this end, students will gain experience in preparing a music proposal suitable for submission to a professional concert or festival, as well as presenting an artists talk.

CAOS202.title: Word and Image
CAOS202.description: This inter-disciplinary subject focuses on dialogue and collaboration between writing and image-making practices.
