HAS100.title: Policing
HAS100.description: This subject will introduce students to the history of policing in historical, political and social contexts, encouraging students to probe definitions of policing and to reflect on the need for public police. Students will explore how the concepts of power, legitimacy and accountability manifest in policing, with particular emphasis on the ways in which these concepts shape diverse policing practice paradigms. Students will consider the impacts of contemporary policing practices, drawing on case study examples

HAS110.title: Introduction to Public Health
HAS110.description: Key historic events have shaped contemporary public health practice, ethics and values. These are continuing to evolve in the face of emerging local and global contemporary public health challenges. In this subject, students will explore the history of the development of public health. They will review conceptual models which inform contemporary public health practice and identify its core ethics and values. Emerging challenges in public health will be investigated, highlighting their role in the production of health inequities. Students will learn how to apply their knowledge of public health practice, ethics and values to critique representations of contemporary public health issues

HAS120.title: Becoming a Social Scientist: Interdisciplinary Competencies
HAS120.description: Social scientists identify, describe and solve social problems. The subject introduces students to the world of social science and provides foundational knowledge and skills to investigate social problems from an interdisciplinary perspective. Students will develop academic literacy, critical thinking and an understanding of ethical approaches from social science perspectives to provide a platform for the rest of the degree program.

HAS121.title: Human Development in Social Context
HAS121.description: Human development is shaped by interactions between the individual and the environment. This subject explores normative human development across the lifespan, from prenatal to adult development and ageing. Major theories of psychosocial development will be covered, and processes of socialisation and identity formation will be highlighted. Ecological systems theory serves as an organizing framework to examine the influence of social environments and relationships at different developmental periods. Variation in development is considered, including empirical research and theory on the influence of social class, culture, socioeconomic status, gender, and other background variables on development.

HAS130.title: Social Determinants of Health
HAS130.description:
Have you ever wondered why some communities or populations have worse health experiences than others? Why, for example, do Indigenous Australians have a shorter life expectancy than the non-Indigenous population? Why are there differences in children’s health depending on where you live in Australia? Why are health related behaviours such as nicotine or alcohol use more prevalent among people from lower socio-economic groups?
Good health is more than the combination of “good genetics and good luck”. The social conditions of our lives exert a powerful influence on our health and wellbeing across our lifespan. Differences in people’s social context- where they are born, live, work and age result in differences in health and wellbeing. Some social contexts result in poor health that is unfair or avoidable.
This subject will challenge you to think about why it’s important to structure our society in ways which allow all people access to health as a human right. We will explore what can be changed to achieve health for all. The course will provide an introduction to key theoretical and methodological concepts that explain health as a social concept. We will also explore some of the important insights and challenges arising from a social determinants of health approach. Throughout the subject, examples will explore health inequities as experienced by some of the most vulnerable and marginalised populations and groups around the globe.

HAS131.title: Introducing Crime and Justice
HAS131.description: The criminal justice system is the primary mechanism through which the state processes and responds to criminal offending. The values that underpin the criminal justice system tell us about our broader social and cultural values, and allow us to locate them within an historical and political context. This subject offers a detailed examination of the institutions of criminal justice - the police, the courts, the penal system and the ways in which individuals and groups are process through them. The subject explores the values and principles that influence the formal administration of justice and the forces that drive vulnerable groups into the justice system at a high rate. Alongside knowledge about the nature and operation of criminal justice, students who complete this subject will develop key skills including an ability to define key criminological concepts, locate and use high quality sources of information about crime and justice, describe and analyse justice processes and their uneven impacts and communicate their developing knowledge in a variety of forms.

HAS150.title: Racism in Australia
HAS150.description:
Australia has been largely formed through ethnocentric, paternalistic and colonial ideologies, including terra nullius. Understanding this and how it shapes current day society is essential to working towards shifting and challenging racism at all levels in society.
This subject will discuss the differing forms of racism, how it affects not only individuals, but whole communities and cultural groups. The subject will discuss the theoretical tools which underpin the continual perpetuation and exclusion of specific groups within society, focussing largely on First Nations’ fight for justice, sovereignty and equal rights.
The subject will challenge students to evaluate their own lens and prejudices, critically analyse structures in society and how we, as a society, can be better.

HAS155.title: International Crime and Justice
HAS155.description: This subject will provide students with an introduction to international crime and justice. The subject is broken into two components: part one will engage with ‘international crime’ – introducing students to the history of international criminal justice and the mechanisms in place to address it (including: the Rome Statute, the ICC, and the relationship between UN human rights instruments and crime). Students will engage with each of the core international crimes including, crimes of aggression, genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes using case studies to illustrate how they are defined, and how they have been responded to in historical and contemporary ways. In part two, the focus will shift to look at ‘transnational crimes’ (for example, human trafficking and slavery, and cybercrime) to illustrate the role of binding and non-binding legal conventions and their relevance to and impact on Australian criminal justice. Across the subject students will evaluate how international crime and justice conceptualisations, legal definitions and crime and justice mechanisms operate to protect international and domestic communities.

HAS200.title: Social Justice in a World of Inequality
HAS200.description: This subject adopts an interdisciplinary approach to studying theories and practices of social justice and social change to address questions about living in a world of inequality. It will investigate how questions of ethics, politics and social justice affect and are affected by diverse forms of knowing, relating and organising for sustainable change. The subject will progress through problem-based inquiry threading broad questions about knowledge, ethics and justice through contemporary problems and issues. Attention will focus on the everyday practices and politics of: respect and recognition; participation and representation; voice and listening; belonging and inclusion; and redistribution. These practices will be investigated in a range of contexts such as ecological and other social movements, community based organisations and international development organisations. Students will explore social justice issues and practices in collaborative contexts involving blogging, peer-to peer presentations and participation in inquiry with social justice organisations.

HAS202.title: Introduction to Social Policy
HAS202.description: Social policy refers to government action that addresses social problems and ensures that human needs are met. This subject considers how social policy in Australia is developed, influenced, and analysed. Various conceptual frameworks are utilized to understand the complex social problems addressed by social policy. Australian political processes are examined, as is the influence of public opinion, the media, and advocacy on policy development. The history and current status of policy in key areas, including health, education, and community services, is explored and critically assessed. Current controversial social issues in Australia are discussed and debated.

HAS205.title: Quantitative Research Design and Analysis
HAS205.description: The subject will prepare students for undertaking analysis of quantitative research data. Students will be introduced to techniques for conducting descriptive and inferential statistical analyses. Students will construct research questions that can be answered by quantitative methods and acquire hands-on experience analysing data and creating data visualisations.

HAS240.title: Introduction to Non-communicable and Communicable Diseases
HAS240.description: This is an introductory subject to noncommunicable (chronic) and communicable (infectious) diseases from an Australian and global context. These conditions are responsible for the vast majority of mortality and morbidity in humankind. Through an interdisciplinary lens, students will explore the dynamics of disease transmission, examining the roles of pathogens, environmental factors and social determinants on vulnerability to both types of disease. Additionally, you will evaluate the efficacy of public health policies and interventions in disease control and prevention

HAS251.title: Introduction to Epidemiology
HAS251.description: The epidemiological approach to the study of disease and illness will be taught. The level of evidence of a number of study types (e.g. cross-sectional, case control, cohort, intervention studies) will be presented in the context of public health problems. Causality and alternate reasons for observed associations (eg. chance, bias, confounding and effect modification) will be discussed. Screening for disease and associated concepts will be discussed. Assessing all these concepts in the evaluation of published studies will be developed. Understanding and calculating measures of disease occurrence and associations with risk factors will be covered and practiced.

HAS259.title: Victimology
HAS259.description:
This subject is delivered across four modules that introduce students to foundational and contemporary perspectives on victimology. Students will explore contested definitions of ‘victim’ from historical, social, and justice perspectives, examining how victim characteristics and the ‘ideal victim’ concept shape societal responses. The subject critically examines how victims’ rights movements have altered the way victims are treated within the criminal justice system, including victim participation frameworks and the risk of secondary victimisation. Students will analyse how victimisation is measured through crime statistics, victimisation surveys and administrative data, reflecting on patterns of crime reporting and underreporting and their implications for understanding victims’ experiences. Through case studies, students will examine diverse victim experiences and develop foundational communication skills for responding appropriately and empathetically to victims of crime. Students will also explore victim support pathways, critically reflecting on barriers to accessing services and how policy frameworks respond to victims’ needs in practice.
Note: This subject contains content that some students may find distressing or triggering, including discussions and case studies related to sexual violence, domestic and family violence, human trafficking and slavery, fraud and financial exploitation. Students are encouraged to engage with course materials with care and access support services if needed.

HAS262.title: Explaining Crime
HAS262.description: This subject offers a comprehensive introduction to major contemporary theories and explanations of crime, examining their foundational assumptions, central hypotheses, and the evidence that supports them. In addition to engaging with individual theories, students will be encouraged to develop a broader capacity for theoretical reasoning—learning to think about outcomes such as criminal behaviour in terms of the complex causal processes that might contribute to them. The subject also considers how criminological theories can be applied to real-world situations, including the interpretation of actual crimes and offender behaviour, and how their relevance and accuracy can be assessed using evidence drawn from practical contexts.

HAS263.title: Crime, Media and Culture
HAS263.description: Crime, Media and Culture explores our cultural fascination with crime and punishment and its representation in a variety of media forms in Australia and internationally. The subject will introduce students to important theoretical concepts, such as moral panics, cultural criminology and contemporary media theory, to help students question why and how our consumption of crime through various forms shapes our knowledge and understanding of crime and the criminal justice system. This subject will cover a range of different media and examples of crime and deviant behaviour, offering opportunities for critical analysis, the impact of cultural criminology on law and social policy, and our emotional responses to crime and violence.

HAS264.title: Crime and Justice in a Digital World
HAS264.description: Crime and Justice in a Digital World introduces students to a specialised, research-led field of enquiry within criminology. The subject begins with consideration of the distinction between crimes that are uniquely ‘online’ or digital in nature, and technology-facilitated crimes that have a long ‘offline’ history. Next, students will consider a series of case studies that critically explore the concept of crime prevention and digital justice in national and international contexts.

HAS315.title: Health Promotion and Communication
HAS315.description: Communication is a key part of health service provision, policy and health promotion. Understanding how we communicate health information, to inform or change behaviour to a variety of people either at an individual or collective level is a vital skill.This subject will focus on the basics of good health communication and health promotion. Health Promotion is the process of enabling people to take control of and improve their health. This subject introduces students to the concept of health promotion and how it has been applied in particular settings such as health services,worksites, schools and communities. This subject will also explore how communication needs to vary depending on the target population including young people, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, the elderly and culturally and linguistically diverse populations. Theoretical perspectives of behaviour change and public policy, as they are applied within the field of health promotion, will also be critically reviewed.By the end of this subject, students will have a better understanding of health communication as well as Health Promotion and will be able to identify, analyse, and apply concepts, theories and methodologies related to health communication in various settings and at various levels of influence.

HAS346.title: Social Advocacy
HAS346.description: This subject prepares students to conduct advocacy for social issues to promote change within communities, systems, and social policy. Students will study the different theoretical frameworks and approaches to advocacy, analyse opportunities and barriers encountered in advocacy actions and debate different advocacy strategies. Students will undertake an advocacy initiative where they will identify a social problem, conduct research, and develop an advocacy plan, including developing advocacy tools. They will identify potential opposition to their advocacy goals and articulate counter arguments. In this process, students will learn skills in persuasive communication, working on teams, and oral communication. Case studies highlight applied approaches to advocacy across a range of issues, including health, education, and social welfare.

HAS353.title: Youth Crime and Justice
HAS353.description: This subject will analyse the experiences that young people have as subjects and resistors of social control, victims of crime and young offenders in conflict with the law. These experiences are contextualised by an appreciation of youth crime and justice as products of historical, theoretical and political junctures which have variously sought to 'protect', 'treat' or 'punish' young people. The subject critically explores young people and social control; considering the boundaries between rights and responsibilities, publics and counter publics, anti-social behaviour and crime and adolescence and adulthood. Next the subject considers young people's connections to crime - as victim-survivors and/or offenders. Finally the subject analyses the system and process of youth justice in Australia. Upon completion of this subject, students will have a portfolio of work which demonstrates their engagement with the variety of ways in which youth, crime and justice are connected.

HAS354.title: Innovative Justice
HAS354.description: This subject analyses and critiques new, innovative approaches to crime, victimisation and social harm. Particular attention will be given to how these innovative approaches are being used to enhance the effectiveness of the formal justice system and communities in dealing with significant issues, such as domestic and sexual victimisation and offending, justice reinvestment and Indigenous over-representation in settler-colonial contexts. Prospective students should note that this subject covers content relating to sexual violence, domestic and family violence, child sexual abuse, colonial and state-perpetrated violence, and armed-conflict violence experienced by civilians. Appropriate support resources and services will be made available, and strategies to recognise the risk of vicarious trauma will be included across the subject, including discussion of self-care and reflective exercises at regular intervals.

HAS356.title: Comparative Social Policy
HAS356.description: This module introduces students to the exciting and challenging subject of Comparative Social Policy. It introduces the key concepts, theoretical frameworks and methodologies used to compare welfare systems. It introduces some of the most up to date research in the field and in so doing focuses on policy developments in an international context. It will demonstrate the usefulness of studying social policy from a comparative perspective . It will introduce conceptual frameworks including path dependency; critical junctures and institutional historicism. It will focus on substantive areas of Australian social policy within the comparative welfare literature on European, US and Asia welfare regimes, exploring their commonalities and differences.

HAS390.title: Community Engagement and Development for Social Change
HAS390.description: This subject offers you a unique opportunity to learn how to engage community, build trust, enlist new resources and allies and create better collaboration within community settings. During this subject, you will learn the process of community engagement and collective action, building productive teams, networking, the use of outreach strategies and facilitating advocacy efforts within the community. Cultural competency and characteristics of community engagement will be also scrutinized to learn ways to efficiently promote engagement in different contexts and settings. Drawing on your knowledge of community engagement theories, methods and ethical principles, you will develop your creative proposal/ idea for community engagement. By the end of this subject, you will identify your personal strengths, struggles, and challenges with community engagement.

HAS401.title: Joint Honours
HAS401.description: The Honours program is designed to provide students with skills to demonstrate excellence in research with a clear understanding of a research question in relation to current knowledge. The degree program fosters the following abilities and skills: plan, design and perform a research project; collect and analyse data; evaluate data; synthesise results and integrate with relevant ideas and concepts; communicate findings; and put relevant OH&S principles into practice. Entry into the Honours program requires the student to have attained at least a credit average in subjects undertaken during their undergraduate degree. The Schools' Honours Coordinator and the prospective supervisor and the Head of School will determine whether a student's 300-level subjects are appropriate for entry into the Honours program. In addition, admission to the Honours program will be dependent upon the availability of an appropriate supervisor, who must be identified by the applicant before applying for entry. Students considering enrolment into Honours should first contact the Schools' Honours Coordinators.

HIST111.title: Age of Revolutions, 1750-1914
HIST111.description: From the mid-eighteenth century, the world was witness to revolutionary political, economic and social changes. Across the globe, people were re-examining the place of religion, education, gender, class, and more in society. They were rethinking democracy, industry, technology and mobility. With the rise of nationalism, new nation-states vied with old empires for their share in global wealth, power and status. Scientific ideas about categories including race were used to underpin group and national identities. In this subject, we examine the unprecedented historical upheaval and revolutionary transformations taking place from 1750 to 1914, the eve of a devastating international conflict, to understand the emergence of the modern world

HIST204.title: Trafficking and Slavery in Global History
HIST204.description: Slavery is a contested term and nowhere more so than in the Asia Pacific. This subject explores the procurement, treatment and resistance of enslaved peoples. It draws on models of slavery from the ancient world and the atlantic slave trade and considers how these relate to later forms of slavery in Australia, Asia and the Pacific Islands. Case studies of child slavery, sexual slavery, domestic and plantation slavery will be considered in colonial, wartime and post-colonial settings. Debates over distinctions between slavery, indentured labour and trafficking will be considered in the context of ongoing abolitionism and the demands of international law.

HIST257.title: The World After 1945
HIST257.description: World War Two shattered Europe and its empires, leaving a world divided between the United States and its Communist rivals, the Soviet Union and China. In the decades that followed 1945, more than one hundred former colonies gained their independence, the Soviet Union rose and fell, and Asia became once more a dominant force in world affairs. It was an era of economic prosperity and environmental challenges, civil and workers' rights, womens' liberation, popular culture, consumerism, and demands for greater freedom and equality. The aim of this subject is to explore the approaches used by historians to understand the complexities of the post-war world.

HIST273.title: Gallipoli Study Tour
HIST273.description: Gallipoli' occupies a significant place in Australia's history. This subject takes students to Turkey and the Peninsula to place 'Gallipoli' within its physical and cultural context. It examines Troy, Constantinople and the Ottoman Empire to provide the broad historical and cultural context for the study tour, the campaign in 1915 with a special emphasis on the Anzac sector and notions of pilgrimage, commemoration and grief. Lectures and seminars provide the introduction to the subject and will be followed by in situ seminars in Turkey and a debriefing seminar on returning to the main campus. Students will spend a week in Turkey.

HIST281.title: Hands-On History
HIST281.description: History is written using the materials that survive to give us clues about the past. This subject considers how historical evidence is created, preserved and used. It provides students with practical experience in accessing primary materials using them to write historical narratives. The subject introduces students to the rapidly growing array of digital tools and resources which are enabling new ways of researching the past.

HIST282.title: Western Front Study Tour
HIST282.description: The Western Front during Great War has been the subject of a growing scholarship over the last decade in both Australia and Europe. This subject examines the 'meanings' of the Western Front and where the Australian experience sits within its broader Allied context by placing students in situ. Sites visited include Verdun, Peronne, Villers Bretonneux, Vimy Ridge, Ipres and other sites in the Somme and Ypres sectors. It is preceded by a week of intensive class preparation followed by approximately six days in the field. Students undertaking this subject are eligible to claim financial assistance ($500) through the Study Abroad Office.

HIST283.title: Film and History
HIST283.description: Film is a powerful tool when it comes to representations of the past, frequently commanding more popular authority than the works of scholars. Books take a long time to read: movies or documentaries are consumed within a matter of hours. But what makes a film 'historical'? Film can reflect the present through the use of the past. Films made in the past offer an interesting insight into their contemporary culture. Documentaries appear to offer historical 'truths'. Film has been used to promote the views of the state through propaganda. Using examples from around the world, this subject examines film as an interpretive tool in historical representation and the use of film as a source of social history. History, rather than the medium of film itself, is the focus of the subject.

HIST293.title: China and the World since 1949
HIST293.description: China’s re-emergence on the world stage has raised concerns about the country’s foreign policy and the impact of its increasing influence in the Asia-Pacific region and around the world. The subject will explore the impact of major political events in China after the proclamation of the People’s Republic in 1949, focussing on her Asian neighbours, Australia and the United States. It provides an overview of Chinese foreign relations since 1949, beginning with the legacies of the “tributary system” and the “century of humiliation” before tracing Chinese involvement with the Cold War, entanglement with other powers, and regional relationships

HIST296.title: Medieval Encounters, 400-1500
HIST296.description: What were the pivotal developments of the medieval period? Why does the medieval world continue to fascinate people today? HIST296 equips students to answer these questions, gaining a deep understanding of the medieval world and its enduring legacy. Focusing on Europe and Asia between 400 and 1500 CE, this subject investigates how trade, religion, warfare, migration, and disease shaped societies and transformed cultural, political, and intellectual life. The subject also explores how the medieval past has been remembered and reimagined in modern popular culture, including in film and video games. Key topics include the spread of world religions, the Silk Road and maritime trade, the Crusades, Mongol expansion, the Black Death, and the rise of witchcraft accusations. The subject culminates with an exploration of the Renaissance—a movement that redefined art and science and laid the foundations for the modern world. Through critical historical analysis, students will develop the ability to interpret medieval sources, critique the work of historians, and assess contemporary representations of the medieval world.

HIST351.title: Australian History: Moments that Matter
HIST351.description: This subject offers a dynamic view of Australian history by highlighting key historical moments that have shaped Australian political, cultural and social life. It explores new approaches to history and areas of research that have emerged in recent times. The subject offers students an opportunity to research areas of personal interest.

HIST357.title: The Making of the Modern Australian Woman
HIST357.description: This subject examines the forces determining the position of women in Australia since the late nineteenth century. It begins with the demographic transition of the 1890s and explores the effects of reduced fertility on marriage and family formation in the twentieth century and how these changes affected the lives of women. How structural change in the Australian economy affected women's life chances by enabling or limiting their education and employment forms is an important area of enquiry, as are political, cultural and social perspectives on the history of women in Australia, and the debates in the historiography of women’s and gender history.

HIST358.title: War and Society
HIST358.description: This subject is thematic in its focus and introduces students to broad questions of war, its nature, its impact on society and its representations through specific examples and using different perspectives. Issues discussed include the definitions and causes of war, biological and social arguments about the existence of war, religion, dispossession, bereavement, commemoration, winners and losers in war, media, propaganda, war crimes, insurgency, genocide, women in combat, war as represented in popular culture and images of war. The specific themes covered vary from year to year. The subject concentrates on war from the nineteenth to the twenty-first centuries and includes contemporary issues.

HIST359.title: Empires Colliding: Britain and USA
HIST359.description: As the British Empire declined, its offspring, the United States, rose. These two world powers were often at odds and yet were inextricably intertwined, politically, economically, culturally. This subject examines the connecting and competing cultures of these imperial ‘centres’ and their colonial ‘peripheries’, from Ireland to India to Cuba. To tell the interconnecting stories of these vast empires, it looks at: violence and resistance; shame and anti-colonialism; worlds’ fairs and imperial might; sport and informal empire; adventure fiction and manliness; humour and traumatic pasts; and, race and immigration controls at the beginnings and ends of empire.

HIST371.title: Modern Dictatorships
HIST371.description: This subject examines the emergence and prevalence of dictatorship as a form of government in the century since World War One.  It explores the practices of the Communist and Nazi states in the light of key themes including imperialism, colonisation, slavery, war and ideology. It asks whether events such as Collectivisation or the Holocaust were unique or are better understood as examples of Genocide. It seeks to understand the impact of the Communist and Nazi states upon ordinary people and how the legacy of Hitler, Stalin and Mao haunt the politics of the present day. It compares present-day examples of dictatorship in China and Russia with their twentieth-century antecedents. Finally, it looks at answers to the question of why dictatorship has proved to be such an enduring challenge to liberal democracy around the globe

HIST387.title: Sex in the Modern World
HIST387.description: Sex has a history. People in the past understood sex, gender and sexuality in different ways. This subject approaches the topic of sex in all of its meanings – desire and sexual identities; reproduction; women's and gender history; constructions of sexual difference and movements for sexual equality. Briefly addressing sex in ancient history, the subject focusses on the modern period - from the late nineteenth century to the recent past. It draws on an array of cross-cultural examples, including but also moving beyond the west, as well as Indigenous perspectives. The subject demonstrates the benefits of taking an historical approach to understanding constructions and experiences of sex. Topics covered include sexual repression and sexual liberation; homosexuality, lesbian, queer and trans identities; masculinities and femininities; reproduction and birth control; prostitution; race and colonialism; suffrage, feminist and #MeToo movements; marriage & domesticity; gender & work; sexual knowledge and sexual revolutions.

HIST396.title: From Lincoln to Trump: Making and Unmaking America
HIST396.description: The end of the Civil War in 1865 ushered in an extraordinary period in American history. Over the next century, the United States became the world’s most powerful empire. Presidents such as Franklin Roosevelt and JFK boasted of extending the principles of freedom and democracy at home and abroad. Yet, democracy within America has always sparked bitter conflict. From the fight to extend voting rights to once enslaved African Americans to Ku Klux Klan terror, to the struggle for women’s suffrage, and the civil rights movement of the 1960s, reform and reaction have characterised the nation’s history. The 2024 election and its aftermath demonstrate that the US is more divided now than at any other time since 1865. By looking at major historical events, foreign relations, domestic politics, and issues such as abortion, gun control, media partisanship, and voting rights, students will learn how and why the US became so powerful and why, despite its divisions, it remains a vigorous influence on our world today.

HIST970.title: Research in History
HIST970.description: HIST970 Research in History explores discipline‐specific issues, through reading, discussion and writing. Students will develop skills specific to the research and writing of history.

HUM030.title: The Art of Understanding: Culture, Communication & Creativity
HUM030.description: This subject invites students on an exploratory journey into the heart of the humanities, focusing on the pivotal roles of culture, communication, and creative/critical thought in shaping human experience. Using an interdisciplinary approach, students will examine the journey of people and societies, engaging with different historical narratives, various forms of communication and expression, and modern/popular culture. This subject aims to ignite a lifelong curiosity in students, encouraging them to question, explore, and reflect upon the ways we understand and interpret the world around us.

HUM900.title: Critical Writing for Contemporary Scholarship
HUM900.description: This module is intended to equip graduate students with a range of compositional and stylistic techniques to enable them to create well-structured introductions, main-content arguments and synopses of secondary literature. This creative process involves familiarization and practice in varied written response pieces, with syntactical and semantic coherence that allow for readability, intelligibility and, crucially, narrative flow. To achieve this, students will be exposed to a range of writing styles on a weekly basis ranging widely from internationally recognized current affairs weeklies (Economist, Newsweek, The Entrepreneur, New Yorker and Foreign Affairs), as well as select academic articles from a range of disciplines (Cultural Anthropology, Culture Studies and Times Literary Supplement). Weekly writing assignments will ensure that students are continuously practicing the art of good writing, which involves lexical variation, powerful introductory clauses, contrasting and comparing academic positions within the same passage while employing ‘the scholarly voice’. Full engagement with this course will advance the students’ ability to organize thoughts as these are put to paper and to avoid writing that depends on itemization and serial quotation without internal narrative cohesion.

HUM907.title: Cultural Studies: Society, Structure and Identity in the Middle East
HUM907.description: The modern Middle East is a diverse geographical and political constellation of societies that seem at once committed to EuroAmerican modernities, and yet resistant to many of the deeper values that underlie these modernities, as evidenced in the localisations of globalization dynamics. In order to understand social and cultural change, the impact of processes of globalisation, issues about urbanism, class, youth, gender, and the nature of social movements and political space, one needs a particular set of diagnostic tools. This course is concerned with the challenge to find such tools through history, anthropology and critical theory.

INDS123.title: Indigenous Geographies: Working with Country
INDS123.description:
'Indigenous Geographies' focuses on the geographic perspectives of Indigenous belonging, reconciliation politics, Indigenous land, and environmental claims and disputes. Content is framed around social and ecological change, introducing students to appropriate ethical, cultural and research skills to respond to social inequities and environmental challenges. The primary focus is Australia, with an overview of the international context. The subject includes colonial history in relation to land, legal and policy processes, and the cultural dimensions of Indigenous relationships to land and environment in urban, regional and remote contexts.
This subject is related to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Find out more: www.uow.edu.au/united-nations-sustainable-development-goals/sdg-subjects-and-courses/

INDS130.title: Indigenous Knowledge in Global Contexts
INDS130.description: INDS130 emphasises the role of Indigenous people as active knowledge producers rather than simply the subjects of other people¿s knowledge. The subject focuses on how Indigenous communities from around the world understand and represent the diversity and complexity of their own lives. It looks specifically at the continuity of Indigenous knowledge systems in relation to family, community, land, water and sky and explores how this knowledge is represented, produced and reproduced in contemporary contexts.

INDS150.title: Introduction to Indigenous Australia
INDS150.description: This subject examines the richness and diversity of Indigenous Australia, focusing on how language, kinship, and connection to place shape identity, belonging, and responsibilities to others. It contrasts colonial projects of classification and control that seek to define who counts as Indigenous with Indigenous perspectives that understand identity as dynamic, relational, and grounded in place. The subject highlights Indigenous sovereignty as embedded in enduring relationships with land and waters, offering alternative frameworks for understanding law, politics, and governance. Students will also analyse how settler colonialism persists as a structure today and explore Indigenous strategies of resistance, renewal, and self-determination.

INDS205.title: Indigenous Peoples and the Environment
INDS205.description: This subject examines the relationships between Indigenous peoples and the environment. Taking a global view and examining a wide variety of case studies this subject focuses on the struggle Indigenous Peoples have maintained to protect their land from encroachment and destruction by settler-colonial forces. Interactions between Indigenous resource systems and Western approaches to conservation and natural resource management will be examined, as well as the links between environmental impacts, policy processes and property regimes.

INDS206.title: Indigenous Arts and Creativity
INDS206.description: Art has been integral to Australian Indigenous cultures for tens of thousands of years. Art has been foundational to the knowledge and expression of Indigenous Ancestral beliefs through origin narratives facilitating the maintenance of law, language and cultural authority. In a traditional context, creative expression can be performative, drawing together multiple forms such as earth sculpture, body painting, rock art, mortuary poles, dance masks and head dresses. Functional objects such as shields, clubs and spears, woven bags, nets and body ornaments are also integral to this context. Contemporary creative expression plays an important role in declaring nationally and internationally the vitality of Indigenous art and culture today, connecting community and Country, while asserting an enduring cultural sovereignty.

INDS207.title: Indigeneity in the Contemporary World
INDS207.description: INDS207 explores how indigeneity is expressed and understood in contemporary global contexts. The subject critically examines a range of perspectives on Indigenous people, their everyday activities and experiences, and the way their lives are represented. It begins by examining how Indigenous people in both the Australian and international contexts have been studied and represented and then investigates how Indigenous people may confirm, challenge or disrupt some of the common expectations about what constitutes "authentic" expressions of indigeneity. Using a number of case studies, the subject will explore how Indigenous people may ‘perform’ their Indigeneity in everyday life; and how, and in what ways, they may symbolize their Indigenous ‘selves’ to others. To what extent are everyday cultural objects and technologies inscribed with new meanings and reworked by Indigenous people in ways that incorporate local knowledges and sensibilities?

INDS208.title: Working with Indigenous Communities
INDS208.description: This subject provides skills to engage and work appropriately and effectively with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities, whether it be as an individual supporter of Indigenous causes, or as professional delivering services or managing at the organisational level. At a personal level, it promotes critical and reflective thinking. At a professional level, it promotes engaging and building relationships with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, communities and organisations. At a service delivery level, it increases awareness of consultation. collaboration and negotiation processes, role-specific issues and resources. For an individual focusing on the organisational level, it provides strategies for enhancing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander employment and developing an organisational approach to improving outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities.

INDS302.title: Indigenous Thinkers: Global Perspectives
INDS302.description: Indigenous Thinkers: Global Perspectives is the Capstone Subject in the Indigenous Studies Major. It introduces students to the different ways Indigenous people understand and represent the diversity and complexity of their own lives, while recognizing that our understandings of Indigenous histories, knowledges, experiences and social realities have been profoundly shaped and, in many cases circumscribed, by those who are embedded in non‐Indigenous systems of knowledge and disciplinary traditions. This subject examines the concepts, theories and sets of meanings that exist at the interface of Indigenous and non‐ Indigenous knowledge systems.

INDS303.title: Indigenous Youth and Popular Culture
INDS303.description: INDS303 introduces students to a range of critical perspectives on Indigenous youth, their activities and experiences, and the way their lives are represented. It explores how Indigenous youth may actively produce, appropriate and consume popular culture and mass-produced consumer commodities to create their own symbolic ‘worlds’ that can provide a sense of identity and belonging.

INDS305.title: Research and Indigenous Communities
INDS305.description: This course examines the methodological, political and ethical challenges that confront both indigenous and non-indigenous researchers who engage in indigenous-centered research in different national and international contexts. The course will consider some of the ongoing debates about power and control of the research process and the generation of knowledge in indigenous contexts. It will critically assess the methodological implications of alternative systems of knowledge and its impact on research practice in both indigenous and non-indigenous settings. The objective of this course is to help equip students to think reflexively about the research process and the challenges of working with and/or for indigenous communities.

INFO411.title: Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery
INFO411.description: Introduction to Data Mining, Knowledge Discovery, and Big Data with coverage of Data Structures, role of Data Quality and per-processing, Association Rules, Artificial Neural Networks, Support Vector methods, Tree Based Methods, Clustering and Classification Methods, Regression and Statistical Methods, Overfitting and Inferential issues, Evaluation, Use of Data Mining packages with applications for benchmark and real world situations.
prerequisites: 36 cp (Knowledge of mathematical and statistical notation at an introductory level.)

rules.description: 36 cp (Knowledge of mathematical and statistical notation at an introductory level.)

INFO412.title: Mathematics for Cryptography
INFO412.description: The subject covers a variety of topics in number theory and their applications to modern cryptography. The number theory studied includes prime numbers, congruences and residues, Euler's phi-function, linear congruences and the Chinese remainder theorem. Elementary group theory is also introduced as a unifying language for number-theoretical concepts and results. We additionally consider more advanced concepts such as lattices and elliptic curves. The cryptographic applications studied include RSA, ElGamal, Rabin, discrete elliptic curve cryptosystems and lattice-based cryptosystems, including the NTRU public key cryptosystem

INTS121.title: Global Politics and Power
INTS121.description: Where does power come from in a globalized world? How can we, as both 'state' and 'global' citizens, make a difference? INTS121 provides an introduction to global politics today. Through the lens of some of the major theories of international relations, we'll explore who matters at the international level, focusing not just on states but also on the multiplicity of other actors who have power to bring about influence and change. We'll also touch on key contemporary global issues including identity, nationalism, human rights, migration, conflict, and the environment. Finally, we'll ask whether the contemporary global order is working and, if not, how we can reform or transform it.

INTS204.title: Global Aid and Development: Challenges and Prospects
INTS204.description: Poverty is still a global scourge and will not disappear without action. This subject provides students with an interdisciplinary introduction to the theoretical approaches, key actors and contemporary issues in international aid and development. It explores what the concept of 'development' means and how historical experience has influenced the evolution of theories of development. It studies the roles of key actors in development, including the state, international organisations, civil society organisations and multinational corporations. In addition, case studies of a range of topical development issues will be undertaken, for example; gender and development, microfinance, rural development, agriculture, environment, and health and sanitation. The subject has a strong practical focus on how aid programs are developed and run, and students will critically assess the successes and failures of projects and evaluate whether aid is effective.

INTS207.title: Conflict, Peace & Security
INTS207.description: The subject examines how issues of security, conflict and peace continue to shape the 21st century. It will: introduce students to the way security has been studied in international relations focusing on a range of security studies approaches; examine the causes and consequences of major recent conflicts; and look at issues surrounding the achievement of peace after conflict. Comparative examples are drawn from Africa, Europe and the Asia Pacific to illuminate the key topic areas. Cross-cutting topics include the influence of great powers, state-building, the rise of the human security paradigm, the role of women in conflict and post-conflict situations and the roles of the UN, military and police in operations.
prerequisites: 36 cp including 6cp of POL or INTS

rules.description: 36 cp including 6cp of POL or INTS

INTS208.title: War and Humanitarianism
INTS208.description: How has war changed and how can the international community help its victims? As the number of wars and other conflicts globally have grown in recent years, we have massive increases in the numbers of civilians killed in conflict while the numbers of displaced persons (including refugees and internally displaced persons) are at the highest levels in seventy years. This subject begins by examining how war has changed, focusing on the significant growth of civil wars as well as other forms of conflict including terrorism and mass atrocities. It then examines how humanitarian actors – including the United Nations, other international and regional organizations, humanitarian non-governmental organizations, and states – seek to work together in these complex emergencies to protect civilians and forced migrants. It will overview both the benefits and pitfalls of the current humanitarian and international legal systems and explore how these mechanisms can be improved.
prerequisites: 6cp of INTS/POL subjects. Students are encouraged to takeINTS207 Conflict, Peace, and Security before enrolling in this subject.

rules.description: 6cp of INTS/POL subjects. Students are encouraged to takeINTS207 Conflict, Peace, and Security before enrolling in this subject.

INTS210.title: Politics of Development
INTS210.description: Building on the basic concepts and theories introduced in INTS204, this subject examines theories and practices related to the development of states. It explores the political, economic, social and cultural dynamics of development by interrogating the key theoretical and practical frameworks that have dominated thinking over the post-World War II period. This includes classical and critical theories of development and practical frameworks like Political Settlements and Developmental States. These theories and frameworks will then be used to explore a number of case studies of states from Asia and Africa. Students will evaluate how the frameworks shed light on the different developmental pathways and objectives of these states. Finally, students will critically reflect on the relationship between development, globalisation and sustainability.

INTS303.title: Australian Foreign Policy
INTS303.description: The subject will provide an in-depth overview of Australia’s role in the world in a range of areas, including culturally, politically, diplomatically, environmentally, economically, geographically, militarily and security. Australia’s relationships with international institutions such as the United Nations, as well as with key states such as the United States and China will also be investigated. Australia’s role in the global arena, in the Indo-Pacific region, and in our immediate neighbourhood will receive particular attention. Students will finish this subject with a comprehensive understanding of Australia’s contributions, limitations and overall place in the world today.
prerequisites: 18cp at 200 levelStudents are encouraged to take INTS 207 “Conflict, Peace and Security” and POL 201 “Australian Politics” before enrolling in this subject (although not compulsory)

rules.description: 18cp at 200 levelStudents are encouraged to take INTS 207 “Conflict, Peace and Security” and POL 201 “Australian Politics” before enrolling in this subject (although not compulsory)

INTS304.title: Gender and International Politics
INTS304.description: This subject considers the role of women and gender in conflict, peace and security.  It covers topics including militarism and the role of masculinity in the military; women in combat, including non-state armed groups; gendered forms of insecurity in conflict-affected settings; and the role of gender in development and peace processes, such as the UNSC’s Women Peace and Security Agenda. Focusing on the debates central to feminist international relations, the subject pays attention to how ideas about gender affect women, men and children’s experiences of conflict and peace, as well as how ideas about gender intersect with sexuality, race and religion.

INTS306.title: The Making of War and Peace
INTS306.description:
This subject examines how responses to modern conflicts and war can lead to peace and security. It explores how different theoretical perspectives within the field of international relations can contribute to our understanding of war and peace. It focuses on why, when, how or sometimes even if, the international community responds to war and conflicts and how state sovereignty can continue to block such efforts.
It also explores the role of key international actors in such responses, including the United Nations system role in diplomacy, peacekeeping, and the Responsibility to Protect. It also examines the role of regional level security initiatives, particularly the development of security mechanisms in the Pacific.
prerequisites: 24 cp at 200 level including 12cp in POL or INTS

rules.description: 24 cp at 200 level including 12cp in POL or INTS

INTS803.title: Australian Foreign Policy
INTS803.description: The subject will provide an in-depth overview of Australia’s role in the world in a range of areas, including culturally, politically, diplomatically, environmentally, economically, geographically, militarily and security. Australia’s relationships with international institutions such as the United Nations, as well as with key states such as the United States and China will also be investigated. Australia’s role in the global arena, in the Indo-Pacific region, and in our immediate neighbourhood will receive particular attention. Students will finish this subject with a comprehensive understanding of Australia’s contributions, limitations and overall place in the world today.

It also explores the role of key international actors in such responses, including the United Nations system role in diplomacy, peacekeeping, and the Responsibility to Protect. It also examines the role of regional level security initiatives, particularly the development of security mechanisms in the Pacific.

INTS807.title: Conflict, Peace & Security
INTS807.description: The subject examines how issues of security, conflict and peace continue to shape the 21st century. It will: introduce students to the way security has been studied in international relations focusing on a range of security studies approaches; examine the causes and consequences of major recent conflicts; and look at issues surrounding the achievement of peace after conflict. Comparative examples are drawn from Africa, Europe and the Asia Pacific to iluminate the key topic areas. Cross-cutting topics include the influence of great powers, state-building, the rise of the human security paradigm, the role of women in conflict and post-conflict situations and the roles of the UN, military and police in operations.

ISIT204.title: Principles of eBusiness
ISIT204.description: This subject aims to provide students with an understanding of eBusiness fundamentals. Today most businesses compete in a global environment and a sound strategy for online business is essential to facilitate this. This subject covers key areas of eBusiness, including: business-to-consumer, business-to-business and business-to-government electronic commerce (EC); online business models and electronic payment systems (EPS) and EC technology basics. Standards, regulation and policy, security and social and economic issues will also be considered in the contexts of business Intranets, Extranets and the Internet. The subject also provides an introduction to the 'Patterns for eBusiness' approach to eBusiness analysis and design.

ISIT207.title: Frontend Web Programming
ISIT207.description: The subject provides students with a practical knowledge of web programming concepts and techniques and user interface design techniques used in the creation of dynamic web sites. The subject will provide students with an opportunity to develop an understanding of the principles of client and server-based scripts as well as user-interface constructs. Students will also be able to apply these principles. The subject provides an in-depth look at the object-oriented features of web programming. Students will have exposure to appropriate software development tools to complete a data cycle of input data store data output data via the web.

ISIT212.title: Corporate Network  Planning and Design
ISIT212.description: The systematic design of networks includes requirements gathering, requirements analysis, the development of logical design and the conversion of the logical design to a physical design. The use of architectures will provide students with a high level framework that consists of addressing and routing, performance characteristics, security and network management. The subject will teach students to relate this framework to basic data communication techniques developed in previous subjects as well extend their knowledge of addressing and routing and performance characteristics.

ISIT219.title: Knowledge and Information Engineering
ISIT219.description: This subject explores issues in using IT to support knowledge sharing and reuse. Challenges in representing and sharing knowledge in the context of deploying knowledge systems are studied. Additional challenges in heterogeneous IT environments are also examined. The subject presents systematic approaches for knowledge engineering via a contemporary Web and modern information modelling approach. The appropriate application environments, acquisition tools and representation schemes for content management are examined along with their relationship to contemporary issues in Web technology.

ISIT224.title: Management Information Systems
ISIT224.description: This subject introduces students to an overview of all the major Information Systems found in a typical business covering systems such as finance, HR, payroll, inventory, sales, CRM, SCM and ERP. Students will be introduced to the processes involved in managing information systems in the contemporary business environment. Students will gain a deep understanding of the issues surrounding the key components of IS (i.e. people, software, hardware, data, and communication technologies), systems and development concepts, technology acquisition, and IT-enabled improvement in quality, speed and agility in modern organisations.
prerequisites: (CSIT113 or CSIT123 or BUS 101) and another 18 credit points at 100 level

rules.description: (CSIT113 or CSIT123 or BUS 101) and another 18 credit points at 100 level

ISIT302.title: Corporate Network Management
ISIT302.description: This subject presents the operational, tactical and strategic issues involved in corporate network management (NM). The subject will introduce a number of NM models e.g. FCAPS, OAM&P etc., and use one of these models to systematically cover the management of: physical components, staff in a network centre, network configuration, user accounts, network performance, security, faults and disasters. The subject also covers concepts such as NM protocols, service level agreements, network integration and the impact of government regulations on NM. These concepts will be reinforced by a series of hands on exercises including using basic network management tools (including scripting).
prerequisites: CSIT127 and 6 credit points at 200 level

rules.description: CSIT127 and 6 credit points at 200 level

ISIT306.title: Strategic eBusiness Solutions
ISIT306.description: This subject aims to provide students with an understanding of how to design integrated solutions for eBusiness using a pattern-oriented approach. Enterprises, both large and small, as well as government institutions, are increasingly becoming reliant upon eBusiness infrastructure. Knowing the strategic business and technology principles and practices related to the design process is becoming increasingly important for a given organisation. This subject will cover business scenarios including electronic data interchange (EDI), supply chain management (SCM), enterprise application integration (EAI), customer relationship management (CRM), sales force automation (SFA); and knowledge management systems (KM).

offerings.display: INTI Subang Jaya-INTI Subang Jaya S1-On-Campus

ISIT307.title: Web Server Programming
ISIT307.description: The subject aims to integrate the previous knowledge which students have gained through subjects on web technologies, web programming and databases to create real-world web applications like shopping carts or advanced form processing systems etc. It also introduces students to open-source programming languages in web development so that they can inexpensively develop sophisticated web applications. Students will become familiar with the integration of programming, databases, web-applications, and structural and object oriented programming.
prerequisites: (CSIT110 or CSIT111) and CSIT115 and CSIT128 and 12 credit points at 200 level

rules.description: (CSIT110 or CSIT111) and CSIT115 and CSIT128 and 12 credit points at 200 level

ISIT312.title: Big Data Management
ISIT312.description: The subject addresses the problems of managing and processing of extremely large data sets in a single-server centralised computing systems and in multi-server clustered and distributed computing systems. The topics related to processing of large data sets in centralised environments include the techniques based on the classical data warehouse technologies such multidimensional data model, data warehouse architecture, data warehouse design both at conceptual and logical levels, and data warehouse processing with appropriate specialised query operations. The topics related to processing of large data sets in distributed environments include the techniques that can be implemented on the clusters of inexpensive computing nodes using MapReduce programming model. The subject introduces the students to the real time analytical processing of large data sets with analytical cluster-based distributed data processing systems. Discussion and hands on exercises related to these topics will equip students to meet the challenges in Big Data environments and appreciate the added challenges of dealing with unstructured data. Students will be presented with opportunities to do hands-on work with appropriate commercial tools.
prerequisites: CSIT115 and 18 credit points at 200 level

rules.description: CSIT115 and 18 credit points at 200 level

offerings.display: UOW at CCCU HK-UOWCHK Sem C-On-Campus

ISIT332.title: Business Process Management
ISIT332.description: Business process management (BPM) combines a process-centric and cross-functional approach to improving how organizations achieve their business goals. A BPM solution makes use of IT to model, automate, manage and optimize business processes to increase productivity. Within this subject students learn important process-centric issues in business system design and implementation. Focus will be placed on both business and technical perspectives of BPM. Topics covered include: Basic business process concepts; Business process modelling; Business process outsourcing; Business process re-engineering; Business process improvement; Workflow and business process automation; Business process management and service-oriented architecture.
prerequisites: CSIT114 and 6 credit points at 200 level

rules.description: CSIT114 and 6 credit points at 200 level

JRNL101.title: News Reporting 1
JRNL101.description: This subject introduces you to journalism and, specifically, news reporting and writing. We will explore the place of news reporting in a changing and evolving journalism landscape. You will consume, analyse and create news content, explore the role of news reporting in a democratic society, and start to develop news reporting and writing skills as part of the journalism program’s student-led publication and broadcast team. Together, as journalism students and new members of the program’s media centre, you will begin to identify and produce university and community-based news stories.

JRNL102.title: News Reporting 2
JRNL102.description: In this subject, you build on the news reporting knowledge and skills explored, discussed and developed in JRNL101 within a workshop environment. You will work independently and as part of a team, including your tutors and senior journalism students, to identify news stories and produce content as part of the journalism program’s media centre. In the workshops, you will consistently identify news stories, pitch them to your editorial leadership team and produce them for potential publication across the UOWTV platforms. You will also reflect on your practice in the workshop environment and publicly via social media and in collaboration with senior journalism students involved in the production of media centre content.

JRNL204.title: Video News and Production
JRNL204.description: This subject focuses on video news reporting and real-time news bulletin production, and builds on the video capture and editing knowledge and skills you developed in JRNL104 Mobile and Social Media Journalism. You will explore the role video plays in the news environment and produce video news content for broadcast on UOWTV as part of the journalism degree’s student-led media centre. You will produce deadline-driven video news content and be involved in studio-based production and broadcast of news bulletins. This subject also encourages you to consider the role and relevance of video news, its audience, and its evolution. You will work independently, as a part of the UOWTV video news production team, and with the student-led media centre’s student editorial leadership members to ensure broadcast accuracy, fairness and quality.

LANG380.title: Language Study Abroad 2
LANG380.description: This subject provides specified credit for subjects in an area of language, literature or civilisation study in French or Indonesian or Italian or Japanese or Mandarin or Spanish undertaken at a university in the country where the language is spoken. Enrolment must be discussed in advance with the convenor of the relevant language program and approved by the Discipline Leader, Languages and Linguistics.
prerequisites: 6cp FREN 200L or 6cp SPAN 200L or permission of the language coordinator

rules.description: 6cp FREN 200L or 6cp SPAN 200L or permission of the language coordinator

LAW101.title: Introduction to Law
LAW101.description: Effective participation in a range of business, political, social, environmental and cultural contexts requires an understanding of legal concepts, processes and institutions. In LAW 101 Introduction to Law, students will gain an understanding of the nature and sources of law, the institutions and processes that underpin the Australian legal system, and the practical skills required to find, use and understand the law. Students also gain foundational knowledge in areas of private law including contract, tort and consumer law, as well as an introduction to criminal law concepts. Upon completion of this subject, students are expected to gain both the knowledge and skills base necessary to pursue further legal studies.

LAW208.title: Public Law
LAW208.description: This subject examines the notion of the state and state power; limitations on state power; the notion of division and separation of powers; mechanisms of accountability and control of government officials, including access to government information, integrity bodies, merits review tribunals and judicial review.

LAW243.title: International Law
LAW243.description: This subject examines the international legal system; its historical and social context; its organisations, including the United Nations, and sources of law, including treaties; its relationship with domestic law; principles of public and private international law; and international dispute resolution. It introduces selected specialist areas including those pertaining to war and crime; land, sea, air, and space; rights and goals; and international commercial and family law.

LAW285.title: Politics of Law and Justice
LAW285.description: This subject introduces students to the study of the intersections of law and justice as foundational components in the framing of social, political, economic, and cultural institutions, with particular emphasis on their constitutional dimensions. Drawing on leading contemporary theories of justice (including utilitarian, liberal, conservative, communitarian, nationalist, socialist, and feminist approaches) and models of democracy (including republican, deliberative, and agonistic approaches), students will critically analyse and evaluate the constitutional design and operation of legal, political, economic, social, and cultural institutions. The subject will therefore provide students with the analytical tools to comprehend how the intersections between law and competing conceptions of justice can either reinforce or destabilise prevailing understandings of lawfulness and its institutional embodiment. Students will also have opportunities to develop cross-disciplinary approaches to critiquing law and justice, while cultivating skills in critical reflection, analysis, and deliberative practice

LAW302.title: Law of Business Organisations
LAW302.description: This subject outlines the key features of the different legal structures which people might adopt for their business and voluntary activities. The legal regulation of three of these - a partnership, a company incorporated under the Corporations Act and a trust as a business structure - are then considered in depth. Practical applications of the law, and public policy dimensions, are addressed throughout the subject.

LAW303.title: Family Law
LAW303.description: The subject examines the legislative framework and common law principles applicable to both the legal recognition of relationships and the resolution of disputes arising from the breakdown of those relationships. Areas covered include: marriage; divorce; nullity; disputes in relation to children under the Family Law Act, 1975 (Cth); property and maintenance disputes for both married and non-married couples; child support and child maintenance; family violence under state and federal legislation; international abduction. The subject also looks at the related areas of state child welfare proceedings and adoption. The course examines what 'family' means today and the challenges our legal system faces in dealing with this fluid concept and recognizing diverse family structures and relationships.

LAW305.title: Health Law
LAW305.description:
This subject will study traditional topics covered by Health Law, including the role of law in patient-doctor relations, covering issues of medical decision-making, confidentiality, privacy, access to information and medical negligence and malpractice, as well as more recent additions, such as regulating emerging reproductive technologies and surrogacy, all through this expanded definition of health. 
A focus on health not just of individuals, but also of communities, populations and nations will also frame the exploration of the legal and ethical challenges that new technologies and a globalized world have brought into this field. How does health law in Australia produce, regulate and co-constitute individuals, communities and populations such as the elderly, Indigenous Australians, people with disabilities, middle class and wealthy populations and people with mental health issues. Finally, the subject will involve study of the role that law, law reform and policy can play in the prevention of illness and the production of a healthy population.

LAW306.title: Privacy Law and Technology
LAW306.description:
While privacy has been valued for centuries, in today’s digital age, there is a resurgence of interest in the legal dimensions of privacy due to the theoretical and practical challenges posed to its protection by new technologies, evolving social norms and the increasing commodification of information. These contemporary developments exert pressure on existing legal frameworks of privacy, to adapt to more complex spatial and informational environments. To engage with these emerging complexities, students of law must cultivate an understanding of the legal and regulatory frameworks of privacy and develop the ability to appraise such frameworks in light of the realities of technological innovation and data-driven markets.
In this subject, students will examine: the meaning and value of privacy from a variety of theoretical perspectives; the historical development of legal privacy protections; the nature and scope of existing frameworks of privacy law in Australia, comprised of a complex mix of both common law and statute; the practical operation of such frameworks in contrast to other comparable jurisdictions; and the interrelationship between law and technology in the pursuit of privacy protection.

LAW309.title: Law and Emerging Technologies
LAW309.description:
Ever wondered what charges might be laid in a deadly traffic accident involving self-driving cars? Or whether it would be an offence if someone traumatised another person in an artificial world? What if a mutant algorithm was linked to a serious crime? And how about the defence options available to someone claiming their brain implant had taken control of their actions?Virtual reality, artificial intelligence (AI), genetic engineering, and military robots are no longer just the realm of science fiction. The rise of – and increasingly dominant social and political role played by – exponential technologies poses serious ethical and legal questions with far-reaching consequences in a vast range of professions including engineering, computer science, health and medicine, psychology, politics, and the media.This hands-on subject is designed to help future-proof your career by teaching you how to identify and learn about new and emerging technologies, while critically analysing their ethical and legal relevance. Working in teams, you’ll use entrepreneurial methods inspired by design thinking to launch a bare-bones version of an original start-up idea that solves a technology-related legal problem for a niche group of customers, users, or beneficiaries. Along the way, you’ll learn why digital literacy, an entrepreneurial mindset, and the ability to engage in “horizon scanning” have become essential for forging a contemporary career regardless of the industry in which you wish to work.
This subject focuses on the criminal, ethical and criminological aspects of emerging and future technologies. If you are interested in Privacy Law, please attend LLB3306 - Privacy Law and Technology subject.

LAW312.title: Law and History
LAW312.description: This subject will provide an examination of the key role that history has played in shaping law and legal institutions over time. A specific focus will be on the historical development of the Australian legal system. The subject begins by providing an historical overview of the development of law by examining systems of the distant past (eg: Babylonian, Greek and Roman law). It then moves on to sketching the antecedents to the Australian legal system, including the British common law tradition. Finally, students will be called upon to critically reflect on dominant discourses of law through time and their impact on cultures or societies. Importantly, the subject seeks to develop a greater understanding of how historical injustices resonate with contemporary issues in law and justice. In doing so, students will conduct an independent research project on the role of law in an example of historical injustice. This can include, but is not limited to, a range of potential themes, including First Nations, gender, sexuality, race or religion.

LAW313.title: Legal Research Project
LAW313.description: LAW 313 Legal Research Project will act as a Capstone opportunity for the Legal Studies major. Under thesupervision of an academic, students will conduct a legal research project and write a 5,000-word paper. LAW313 provides students with the opportunity to evaluate a current issue associated with a particular area of lawand apply critical and problems solving skills to address the selected topic.

LAW314.title: Climate Change, Sustainability and the Law
LAW314.description: This subject focuses on the role of the law in relation to climate change and key related sustainability issues. It considers the legal role and responsibilities of individuals, governments and businesses in tackling these issues, including the concept of corporate social responsibility. The subject considers key concepts relating to climate change and sustainability laws, including ecologically sustainable development and climate change mitigation and adaptation, as well as some of the underlying scientific, economic and policy debates as they relate to law. The subject examines key international legal instruments relating to climate change as well as the legal and related policy responses within Australia, particularly at Commonwealth and State level. Climate change litigation is also examined, with a particular focus on litigation against governments and business. Crime and other contraventions in the context of climate change are also explored. Related sustainability issues such as the circular economy, sustainable waste management and plastics pollution are also examined from a legal perspective. Other contemporary issues relating to climate change and sustainability may also be considered.

LAW316.title: Work Health and Safety Law
LAW316.description: This subject is concerned with the study of the legal regime governing health, safety and welfare of people at work. Its focus will be the model Work Health and Safety Act 2011, Work, Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) and the Model Work Health and Safety Regulations 2012.

LAW319.title: International Business Law
LAW319.description: This subject will contain some selected legal and regulatory frameworks of international business.
