Thermodynamic systems; equations of state; work; the first law of thermodynamics and its consequences; the second law of thermodynamics; entropy; combined first and second laws; thermodynamics potentials; applications of thermodynamics; kinetic theory of the ideal gas; molecular velocity distribution.

PHYS236.title: Classical Mechanics
PHYS236.description: Classical Mechanics provides a foundational understanding of the laws governing motion, forces, energy, and momentum. This subject builds the theoretical framework for advanced subjects such as electromagnetism, quantum mechanics, and relativistic physics. Students develop strong analytic and problem-solving skills through mathematical modelling, lab practical/simulation, and physical interpretation.

PHYS254.title: Climate Change, Energy and Sustainable Societies
PHYS254.description:
This subject develops students' mathematical literacy and understanding of key physics concepts related to energy and climate change. It examines the physics of different forms of energy supply and evaluates strategies to decarbonise societies. The subject will also assist students in the evaluation of claims about climate change, energy resources and sustainability.
PHYS254 addresses United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 7,8,9,11,12 and 13, and develops students' intercultural competence through examination of Indigenous perspectives on sustainable societies.

PHYS255.title: Nuclear and Radiation Physics
PHYS255.description: Module I covers core concepts of radiation physics, including radiation (photons, charged particles and neutrons) interactions with matter and radioactive decay. Module II covers core concepts of nuclear physics, including nuclear size, nuclear mass, binding energy, nuclear force, nuclear structure and nuclear shell models. The Module concludes with an overview of particle accelerators and their applications in industry.

PHYS295.title: Astronomy - Concepts of the Universe
PHYS295.description: This subject takes a non-mathematical approach to Astronomy. No prior knowledge of physics is required to do the subject. This course will illustrate the techniques used by astronomers and will attempt to give an understanding of the universe as we presently understand it. The use of telescopes will give the opportunity to observe the phenomena discussed. The development of astronomy; the planets; the formation of the solar system; the sun as a star; the message of starlight; the visible stars; the birth and death of stars; telescopes, big and small; the milky way; the universe of galaxies.

PHYS305.title: Quantum Mechanics
PHYS305.description: The course is an introduction to the wave mechanical theory of quantum mechanics and some applications to simple systems. Probability, the Wave Function, Schrodinger's equation in one dimension, normalisation, expectation values, operators. The time-independent Schrodinger equation, application to various potential functions, tunnelling. QM in three dimensions, degeneracy, the hydrogen atom. Time independent perturbation theory, angular momentum and spin, identical particles; atoms, solids and quantum statistics.
prerequisites: PHYS205 and PHYS235 and either MATH202 or MATH283

rules.description: PHYS205 and PHYS235 and either MATH202 or MATH283

PHYS306.title: Project in Physics
PHYS306.description: Option 1: After successfully completing this subject, the student will be able to design and construct experiments appropriate to undergraduate physics programs and be able to document the procedure required for carrying out such experiments. Option 2: After successfully completing this subject, the student will have gained experience in working as part of a small research group be able to keep working records of the progress of experiments have gained a variety of basic skills related to the specific area of research in which they have been involved.

PHYS325.title: Electromagnetism
PHYS325.description: Starting with the Maxwell field equations, the course examines the properties of electromagnetic waves in free space, non-conducting and conducting materials, waveguides and plasmas. Reflection and refraction, particularly total internal reflection, are covered in detail. The generation of electromagnetic waves by accelerating charge is treated via the Lienard - Wiechert potentials and Feynman's equation. Revision of charge continuity, Maxwell's equations, boundary conditions. EM waves in free space and materials. Reflection and refraction, Snell's law and the Fresnel equations, total internal reflection and evanescent waves. Waveguides, TE and TM modes, cut off frequency. Generation of EM waves, Lienard-Wiechert potentials, Feynman equation and its application to simple systems: far-field dipole and synchrontron radiation fields.

PHYS385.title: Statistical Mechanics
PHYS385.description: Content: This course on the basic theory of Statistical Mechanics covers: the quantum state of a system of particles, ensembles, multiplicity functions, system in contact, energy and particle exchange, entropy and temperature, Gibbs and Boltzmann factors, partition functions, fluctuations, identical particles, classical and quantum gases, blackbody radiation, the Debye theory of solids and phonons, Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics, electrons and holes in semiconductors and an introduction to superconductivity.

PHYS396.title: Electronic Materials
PHYS396.description: In this subject, the following topics relevant to the nature of electronic materials will be covered: Atomic bonding and crystal structure. Electrons in solids, band theory: insulators, conductors, semiconductors and superconductors. The free and nearly free electron theories. Electrical conductivity, Hall effect. Types of magnetic materials. Semiconductors - intrinsic, extrinsic, the hole, the p-n junction. Superconductors - phenomena, BCS theory. Production of semiconductors and superconductors, control of processing to achieve desired properties. Design and production of novel materials to achieve improved performance in electronic devices; modern applications.

PHYS457.title: Research Project
PHYS457.description: Content: The student will be required to participate in a research program on a physics topic under the supervision of a staff member. The student will have a choice of the following fields: Nuclear Medicine, Medical Imaging, Radiobiology, Radiation Protection, Diagnostic Radiology, Pathology and Imaging Physics, Astronomy, Solid State Physics. All the above research topics may not be available every year.
prerequisites: 24 cp of third year subjects from the BMedical Physics or BSc (Physics).
corequisites: 24 cp of fourth year subjects from the BMedical Physics or BSc (Honours).
degree_restrictions: Only available to students in course codes 1815, 357, 358,  380 or 480

rules.description: 24 cp of fourth year subjects from the BMedical Physics or BSc (Honours).
24 cp of third year subjects from the BMedical Physics or BSc (Physics).

PHYS462.title: Medical Imaging
PHYS462.description: Diagnostic image acquisition techniques, image analysis in quality assurance and artefacts. Topics covered will include - the photographic process, solids state detectors and CCDs, the hardware of image processing; film digitisers and plate scanners, software techniques, histograms, enhancements, convolution, edge enhancement, fourier techniques and operature synthesis, Sources of diagnostic X - rays, computer tomography, instrumental set up, image definition, back projection, signal to noise, CT numbers, contrast, CT and radiotherapy. Principles of, and quality assurance in ultrasound imaging. Nuclear magnetic resonances, Larmor frequency, basic imaging, slice selection, phase and frequency encoding, spin echoes, TE and TR relaxation times, mechanisms of contrast in MRI, multiecho imaging, multi slice imaging, fast imaging, flow imaging. MR angiography, 3D data acquisition, chemical shift imaging, contrast agents, image artifacts and distortion, localised spectroscopy, set up of a clinical MR scanner, safety aspects.
prerequisites: 24 cp of third year subjects from the BMedical Physics program including PHYS255.
degree_restrictions: Only available to students in course codes 1815, 357, 358, 380 or 480.

rules.description: 24 cp of third year subjects from the BMedical Physics program including PHYS255.

PHYS463.title: Nuclear Medicine
PHYS463.description: The contents of this subject cover fundamental knowledge of nuclear medicine physics. It has been developed by medical physicists registered with the ACPSEM as Qualified Medical Physics Specialists in nuclear medicine with the aim to fulfil the requirements for Level 1 competency of the ACPSEM Diagnostic Imaging Medical Physics training program (Nuclear Medicine module). The subject is structured into 2 parts: part I covers physics knowledge of the imaging acquisition processes and equipment, discuss image quality and image quality controls, discusses absolute quantification of nuclear medicine images and introduces tracer kinetics. Part II applies the concepts learnt in part I to clinical nuclear medicine investigations and therapies. It introduces some examples of the clinical indications and physiological processes investigated in nuclear medicine, focussing in particular on image acquisition and processing of dynamic images. Part II includes basic computer science knowledge necessary in nuclear medicine, dosimetry techniques for population and patient specific dosimetry of internal radionuclides and awareness of radiation protection (practical considerations and regulatory requirements) in nuclear medicine.
prerequisites: 24 cp of third year subjects from the BMedical Physics program including PHYS255
degree_restrictions: Only available to students in course codes 1815, 357, 358, 380 or 480.

rules.description: 24 cp of third year subjects from the BMedical Physics program including PHYS255

PHYS961.title: Radiation Protection and Radiobiology
PHYS961.description: Topics covers in this subject include - Interaction of radiation with living cells and tissue; clinical fractionation; clinical radiation syndromes; radiobiological modelling; experimental radiation oncology; local control vs system control; radionuclide therapy; binary therapy; new radiotherapy modalities and their radiobiology; dosimetry; natural background radiation; principles of radiation protection; instrumentation for radiation protection; Radiation protection in radiation therapy and diagnostic settings.

PHYS962.title: Medical Imaging
PHYS962.description: Diagnostic image acquisition techniques, image analysis in quality assurance and artefacts. Topics covered will include - the photographic process, solids state detectors and CCDs, the hardware of image processing; film digitisers and plate scanners, software techniques, histograms, enhancements, convolution, edge enhancement, Fourier techniques and operature synthesis, Sources of diagnostic X - rays, computer tomography, instrumental set up, image definition, back projection, signal to noise, CT numbers, contrast, CT and radiotherapy. Principles of, and quality assurance in ultrasound imaging. Nuclear magnetic resonances, Larmor frequency, basic imaging, slice selection, phase and frequency encoding, spin echoes, TE and TR relaxation times, mechanisms of contrast in MRI, multi-echo imaging, multi slice imaging, fast imaging, flow imaging. MR angiography, 3D data acquisition, chemical shift imaging, contrast agents, image artifacts and distortion, localised spectroscopy, set up of a clinical MR scanner, safety aspects.

PHYS963.title: Nuclear Medicine
PHYS963.description: The contents of this subject cover fundamental knowledge of nuclear medicine physics. It has been developed by medical physicists registered with the ACPSEM as Qualified Medical Physics Specialists in nuclear medicine with the aim to fulfil the requirements for Level 1 competency of the ACPSEM Diagnostic Imaging Medical Physics training program (Nuclear Medicine module). The subject is structured into 2 parts: part I covers physics knowledge of the imaging acquisition processes and equipment, discuss image quality and image quality controls, discusses absolute quantification of nuclear medicine images and introduces tracer kinetics. Part II applies the concepts learnt in part I to clinical nuclear medicine investigations and therapies. It introduces some examples of the clinical indications and physiological processes investigated in nuclear medicine, focussing in particular on image acquisition and processing of dynamic images. Part II includes basic computer science knowledge necessary in nuclear medicine, dosimetry techniques for population and patient specific dosimetry of internal radionuclides and awareness of radiation protection (practical considerations and regulatory requirements) in nuclear medicine. The structure of the subject is as follows: Part I: 1. Review of physics concepts relevant to nuclear medicine 2. Principles of tracer kinetics 3. Gamma camera 4. Single Photon Emission Tomography 5. Positron Emission Tomography 6. Absolute Quantification in planar and tomographic images Part II: 7. Clinical nuclear medicine investigations 8. Computing in nuclear medicine 9. Dynamic imaging 10. Radiation dosimetry in nuclear medicine 11. Radiation protection in nuclear medicine

PHYS965.title: Detection of Radiation
PHYS965.description: Starting with theory of radiation dosimetry for electrons and photons, it explores the definition of absolute dose and radiation dose measurement protocols. The course examines the concept of relative dose measurement and properties of ionization chambers and their design principles. Semiconductor detectors and their response to radiation is developed for different applications including medical radiation physics. Other dosimetry technology are explored including Thermoluminescent dosimeters, radiochromic and Gafchromic film, chemical dosimeters and their application in dosimetry.

PHYS966.title: Physics of Radiotherapy
PHYS966.description: This subject will lead to an understanding of the instrumentation and techniques involved in diagnostic and therapeutic uses of radiation in medicine. Topics covered will include Interactions of Radiation with Matter, Sources of Radiation, Detecting Radiation, Nuclear Electronics and data acquisition system, Nuclear Reactions and Production of Radioisotopes, Neutron Physics, Dosimetry of photons, electrons and neutrons, Solid Sate Dosimetry, TLD and film dosimetry, Introduction to Radiation Therapy, Medical Linear Accelerators, X-ray Modelling Methods, Brachytherapy and Radiosurgery, Clinical Radiotherapy, Linear Accelerators X-ray and Electron Beam Properties.

PHYS967.title: Research Project
PHYS967.description: In this subject students will be assigned a topic from their School's academic staff in an area that is related to their coursework degree. Students will be provided with instructions on how to research and develop a literature review and a project proposal related to the topic in small groups who have a common research theme. At the end of the session, the student is required to produce a written report and a seminar presentation on the respective topic.

PHYS969.title: Electronic Materials
PHYS969.description: In this subject, the following topics relevant to the nature of electronic materials will be covered: Atomic bonding and crystal structure. Electrons in solids, band theory: insulators, conductors, semiconductors and superconductors. The free and nearly free electron theories. Electrical conductivity, Hall effect. Types of magnetic materials. Semiconductors - intrinsic, extrinsic, the hole, the p-n junction. Superconductors - phenomena, BCS theory. Production of semiconductors and superconductors, control of processing to achieve desired properties. Design and production of novel materials to achieve improved performance in electronic devices; modern applications.

POL150.title: Government, Power and Political Systems
POL150.description: POL 150 is a broad comparative subject that aims to embed fundamental concepts that are essential to the study of politics: citizen, individual, gender, class, race, state, government, civil society, political parties and systems, as well as international organisations and institutions. It draws on Australian, Asia-Pacific, American, and European examples to illuminate specific issues in domestic, comparative and global politics.

POL201.title: Key Concepts in Political Thought
POL201.description: The aim of this subject is to examine a range of political concepts and theories, and to expand the scope of what should be counted as part of “the political”. Rather than limit our understanding of “the political” to formal systems of power and authority and the ideologies that represent these systems, in this subject we understand “the political” as the public field where rule and domination are problematised. Hence, “the political” refers to the multiplicity of forces, structures, problems, and orientations that shape our collective life. We enter the frame of “the political” wherever our lives together are staked and wherever collective action could make a difference to the outcome.In this context, political concepts are conceived in this subject as a forum for conversation and constructive debate rather than the construction of an encyclopaedic ideal. Some of the concepts we will be exploring are: regime, democracy, capitalist reproduction and social reproduction, neoliberalism and social insecurity, debt, patriarchy, political violence, coloniality and decolonisation, surveillance capitalism, racial resentment, and more.
prerequisites: 36cp including 6cp POL or 36cp including 6cp PHIL or 36cp including 6cp INTS

rules.description: 36cp including 6cp POL or 36cp including 6cp PHIL or 36cp including 6cp INTS

POL202.title: Politics in the USA
POL202.description: This subject examines the American political system. It provides an introduction to the institutional context of American politics, focussing upon the structure and function of government, and also deals in depth with major factors and issues which shape politics today. The roles, in theory and practice, of the Constitution, the President, the Congress, the Supreme Court are examined. Political parties, election processes and campaigns are surveyed and analysed. These institutional aspects of American politics raise crucial questions about democracy and power, questions which the subject deals with at length.
prerequisites: 36cp including 6cp POL at 100 level or 36cp including 6cp INTS

rules.description: 36cp including 6cp POL at 100 level or 36cp including 6cp INTS

POL204.title: Politics and the Media
POL204.description: This subject examines the political impacts of media on the public sphere. Particular attention is paid to the role of counter-publics, the construction of news frames, and how social media and the internet shapes participation in C21st politics.  We focus on news reporting and commentary, including textual and visual, (photography, film and podcasts).  The subject engages with cultural politics in general including popular culture.

POL304.title: Power and the State
POL304.description: Power and the State is the capstone subject in the Politics major. It charts the rise of the state from its origins to its dominant role in everyday national life. Writers examined may include, inter alia, Tilly, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Rousseau, Burke, Marx, Weber, TH Green, Gramsci, Althusser, Foucault, Marshall, and Agamben. Through blogs and a major research project students will explore the relation of the individual to the state and the balance between liberty and state power.
prerequisites: 24cp at 200 level including 12cp of POL or INTS

rules.description: 24cp at 200 level including 12cp of POL or INTS

POL306.title: Complex Peace Operations
POL306.description: This subject examines international responses to modern conflicts across the world. It focuses on why, when, how or sometimes even if, the international community responds. It addresses issues surrounding the UN system of peacekeeping, as well as unilateral and regional interventions, and the new emphasis on protecting human rights as part of the broader responsibilities of statehood and modern sovereignty.
prerequisites: 24 cp at 200 level including 12cp in POL or INTS

rules.description: 24 cp at 200 level including 12cp in POL or INTS

POL309.title: Global Political Economy
POL309.description: The subject covers the development of Political Economic theory from antiquity to the present day. The centrality of political economy to political enquiry is stressed. It discusses major theorists from Plato, Quesnay, Adam Smith, Karl Marx and John Maynard Keynes to contemporary thinkers, debates and issues. It analyses core aspects of their approach to key political questions, such as: the role of the modern state, human nature, social order, civil society, freedom and necessity, production, distribution and justice. It questions the relevance of their thought to a range of contemporary issues in a (post)-modern environment.
prerequisites: 24cp at 200 level including 12cp INTS or POL

rules.description: 24cp at 200 level including 12cp INTS or POL

POL311.title: Politics of the Middle East
POL311.description: The aim of this subject is to offer students a chance to engage and grapple with the most important debates that dominate the recent history and contemporary politics of the Middle East and to locate and conceptualise these debates within the wider context of world politics. A special focus will be devoted to the study of historical Palestine, and of Israel-Palestine politics.
prerequisites: 24cp at 200 level including 12cp POL or INTS

rules.description: 24cp at 200 level including 12cp POL or INTS

POL326.title: Global Inequality
POL326.description: Contemporary globalisation has seen the intensification of inequality between, as well as within, developed and developing nation-states. This subject investigates the politics of global inequality through historical, structural and everyday-life lenses. The main focuses are the relations between the Global North and South, the rich and poor across the world and inequality within nations. Issues examined may include: the historical construction of North-South relations, processes of inequality and its transmission, transnational aid, the liberalization of trade, production and social reproduction, the global mobility of labour and conflicts over resources.
prerequisites: 24 CP at 200 level including 12CP of POL or INTS

rules.description: 24 CP at 200 level including 12CP of POL or INTS

POL809.description: The subject covers the development of Political Economic theory from antiquity to the present day. The centrality of political economy to political enquiry is stressed. It discusses major theorists from Plato, Quesnay, Adam Smith, Karl Marx and John Maynard Keynes to contemporary thinkers, debates and issues. POL826.description: Contemporary globalisation has seen the intensification of inequality between, as well as within, developed and developing nation-states. This subject investigates the politics of global inequality through historical, structural and everyday-life lenses. The main focuses are the relations between the Global North and South, the rich and poor across the world and inequality within nations. Issues examined may include: the historical construction of North-South relations, processes of inequality and its transmission, transnational aid, the liberalization of trade, production and social reproduction, the global mobility of labour and conflicts over resources.

PSYC101.title: Introduction to Behavioural Science
PSYC101.description: This subject provides an introductory overview of areas of psychological investigation, introducing students to the study of key psychological concepts and their applications. While the aim of the course is to acquaint non-psychology majors with the discipline, it also provides additional background information to students intending to specialise in psychology. The course will introduce students to the major areas of study in the science of psychology, covering topics such as learning, cognition, motivation, emotion, personality, and lifespan development.

PSYC120.title: Critical Thinking and Communication Skills in Psychology
PSYC120.description: PSYC120 delivers a holistic overview of the requirements for the successful completion of an undergraduate degree in Psychology at UOW. This course will cover a broad range of topics and contextualise course content. It will highlight core concepts in psychology. It will present a science-focussed approach to psychology that will link psychological research with its broader role in evidenced-based clinical practice. It will provide key skills aimed at engaging students in core content, course material and readings and provide practical training that will allow students to develop independent learning skills. It will also provide writing and research skills that they will require throughout their undergraduate degree. It is expected that students completing this course will be able to understand what will be required of them throughout their undergraduate degree.

PSYC121.title: Foundations of Psychology A
PSYC121.description: This subject is a prerequisite for enrolment in second year psychology subjects. With PSYC120, PSYC122 and PSYC123, it comprises an introduction to theories and practical skills in psychology. It introduces students to the science of psychology. The content will focus on the way the individual's biological and psychological systems function. In particular, the subject will examine the historical context of psychology, biological bases of human behaviour, lifespan development, motivation and emotion, stress and health, personality, assessment, states of consciousness, and indigenous and cultural psychology.

PSYC122.title: Foundations of Psychology B
PSYC122.description: This subject is a prerequisite for enrolment in second year psychology subjects. The subject examines the way in which individuals perceive and learn about their world, the ways in which group membership influences behaviour, the nature of psychological dysfunction, and the role of psychology in influencing health. Topics covered include learning, perception, intelligence, memory, cognition, psychology of abnormality, social psychology, and human relations.

PSYC123.title: Research Methods and Statistics
PSYC123.description: This subject is a prerequisite for enrolment into second year psychology subjects. Together with PSYC121 & PSYC122, it provides an introduction to the theories and practical skills characteristic of scientific psychology. The course has two main components: research methods and statistics. The methods component covers the scientific method, role of theories and hypotheses, research design, experimental comparisons, correlation and causation, reliability and validity, and ethical and cultural considerations. The statistical component provides an introduction to statistical reasoning as well as to elementary statistical procedures including: descriptive statistics, graphical representation of data, sampling and the normal distribution, and the use and interpretation of statistical tests of association and mean comparison.

PSYC216.title: Foundations of Sport and Exercise Psychology
PSYC216.description: The objective of PSYC216 is to identify, explain and apply the foundational principles of sport and exercise psychology across a broad range of sport and exercise settings. The key skills that students will learn are to critically examine the ways that multiple principles may apply to any particular situation, and to design and evaluate effective and evidence-based interventions. The subject has a dual focus on exercise psychology (e.g., why people become physically active) and sport psychology (e.g., why some people perform well under pressure), as well as key principles that cut across both fields (e.g., motivation, goal setting). Lectures will cover the foundational principles, while tutorials and assessment tasks are designed to help students to apply those principles in practice.

PSYC231.title: Personality
PSYC231.description: This subject will provide students with an understanding of the past and current theories in personality development, theories and change. For the personality theories relevant current research will be highlighted. Related areas of individual differences will be covered including measurement issues in personality, personality culture, situation, stability and change will also be covered. Additionally the major issues in intelligence and its measurement will be outlined.

PSYC234.title: Biological Psychology and Learning
PSYC234.description: This subject will begin to examine the biological mechanisms underlying behaviour and changes in behaviour brought about by experience, as well as examining the psychophysiological and behavioural measures frequently employed to study these processes. Topics will include genetics, the nervous and endocrine systems, arousal, attention, learning, memory, language, Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning, habituation and orienting reactions. The practical component will include an introduction to the techniques and experimental methods used in the study of learning and psychophysiology, including the recording of the electrocardiograph, skin conductance, and the electroencephalograph.

PSYC236.title: Cognition and Perception
PSYC236.description: This subject provides an overview of two broad content areas in experimental psychology. Perception is the study of how information is acquired from the environment through sensory organs. Cognition is concerned with the storage, manipulation and retrieval of such information. Lectures draw upon findings from both behavioural and neuropsychological studies. Topics covered include visual perception, attention, memory, language. Students learn how to conduct, analyse, and interpret experimental research.
prerequisites: PSYC120, PSYC121, PSYC122, PSYC123 and PSYC250

rules.description: PSYC120, PSYC121, PSYC122, PSYC123 and PSYC250

PSYC241.title: Developmental and Social Psychology
PSYC241.description: This subject discusses core issues in child, adolescent and adult development with an emphasis on behaviour in the perceptual, cognitive, and social environment. Half of the subject will provide a developmental framework from the neonatal stage through adulthood. Key theories and empirical aspects in perceptual, cognitive and emotional development will be covered. Ethical issues concerning research involving children will also be addressed. The second half emphasises the contributions of social psychology to understanding individual behaviour in societal context including the workplace. The development of the social self, attitudes, prejudice and the importance of social cognition will be covered. The implications of issues arising from these core topics to indigenous psychology will also be considered.

PSYC250.title: Quantitative Methods in Psychology
PSYC250.description: This subject will give you a solid basic knowledge in data analysis techniques for simple experimental designs and correlational studies. These techniques will be developed around an understanding of experimental and quasi-experimental methods. Considerable attention is given to explaining the conceptual rationale underlying each analysis covered in the subject and its application to research in the behavioural sciences. The need for critical evaluation of AI-generated statistical outputs and interpretations will be discussed. The content of the practical classes entails extensive use of SPSS and/or jamovi, computer-based statistical packages.
prerequisites: PSYC120, PSYC121 and PSYC122 and PSYC123

rules.description: PSYC120, PSYC121 and PSYC122 and PSYC123

PSYC251.title: Psychopathology
PSYC251.description: This subject takes a developmental approach to mental health issues. It seeks to examine some of the common factors leading to these issues in both childhood and adulthood. An introductory exploration of the most prevalent issues is undertaken, using a variety of therapeutic models.

PSYC324.title: Assessment and Intervention
PSYC324.description: This subject provides students with an overview of widely used psychological assessment procedures (including personality and intelligence assessments). Intervention programs and their efficacy will also be discussed, as well as ethical and legislative requirements and consumer and carer participation. Areas of focus will include both clinical and non clinical settings. The subject will also deal with the counselling process by introducing students to basic interviewing skills used in counselling. Seminar and Workshop Sessions will provide students with an opportunity to observe counselling micro-skills and participate in group discussions and seminars.
prerequisites: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC231 and PSYC241

rules.description: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC231 and PSYC241

PSYC325.title: History and Philosophy of Psychology
PSYC325.description: This subject introduces (1) the origins and development of major approaches in modern psychology, and (2) important conceptual issues in psychology. It discusses the types of critical analysis needed to evaluate the theories, methods, accounts and practices that we encounter in psychology, and applies these to various psychological problems. Topics include: the place of history and metatheory in the study of psychology; science, mind and knowledge in the classical and medieval world, and in the early scientific era; rationalist and empiricist accounts of mind and knowledge; the legacy of empiricism and reactions to it; the 19th century, evolution, the beginning of empirical and experimental psychology; the development of the orthodox view of science and its influence on psychology; behaviourism; debates on science, its growth and status; contemporary psychologies from constructivism to cognitivism, functionalism and the computational model; realism.

PSYC326.title: Design and Analysis
PSYC326.description: PSYC326 develops skills in the design and analysis of research investigations involving statistics. It is a pre-requisite for entry into Psychology Honours. Statistical computing is an essential part of the course. Topics covered: statistical techniques in psychological research, experimental and observational research designs, analysis of survey data; analysis of variance and covariance; regression; factor analysis; multivariate analysis; logistic regression.
prerequisites: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC250

rules.description: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC250

PSYC327.title: Advanced Topics in Cognition
PSYC327.description: This subject offers more advanced training in experimental psychology, and particularly the method and theories of cognitive psychology. It is one of the subjects that provides a solid grounding in empirical psychology. The subject will extend students' knowledge of cognitive psychology from the framework acquired in PSYC236. It provides a detailed examination of a number of areas which may include short-term-memory, the psychology of reading, face recognition and reasoning. The practical program involves extensive experience of experimentation in cognitive psychology where students will act both as participants and researchers. Some of these experiments will be written up as lab reports or short assignments.
prerequisites: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC236 and PSYC250

rules.description: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC236 and PSYC250

PSYC328.title: Visual Perception
PSYC328.description: Perception is essential for our successful interaction with the world around us. Vision is one of our most important senses – allowing us to perceive characteristics of objects and surfaces at large distances beyond our reach. This subject covers the following topics: (1) the physiological bases of visual perception; (2) the visual perception of shape, colour, motion, size and depth; (3) the perception of objects and faces; (4) interactions between vision and the other senses (perceiving self-motion, self-orientation, and control of balance); (5) some clinical and applied issues. Students will be exposed to the ethical use of state-of-the-art experimental techniques and digital technologies (virtual reality, GenAI, etc.).
prerequisites: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC236 and PSYC250

rules.description: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC236 and PSYC250

PSYC329.title: Psychophysiology
PSYC329.description: This subject concentrates on psychophysiology as the systematic examination of peripheral and central physiological correlates of perceptual and cognitive functioning. Students will attain a basic level of proficiency in the electrical recording and assessment of a range of autonomic measures (including muscle, respiratory, cardiovascular, and electrodermal activity), as well as the traditional central indicators (EEG and event related potentials). Current research using these techniques will be examined.
prerequisites: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC234 and PSYC250

rules.description: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC234 and PSYC250

PSYC330.title: Social Behaviour and Individual Differences
PSYC330.description: This subject allows students to study selected topics in social behaviour in more detail. The emphasis is on the extent to which one can explain social behaviours (eg. prejudice, crime, close relationships, particular adolescent behaviours) on the basis of individual differences and personality traits. An integral part of the subject will include the formulation of a research proposal by each student.
prerequisites: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC231, PSYC241 and PSYC250

rules.description: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC231, PSYC241 and PSYC250

PSYC357.title: Forensic Psychology
PSYC357.description: This subject introduces students to the interactions between psychology and the law, specifically focussing the role of the forensic psychologist. It includes a variety of lectures and interactive tutorials covering topics including core legal issues around criminal responsibility and giving expert evidence in court, as well as more applied topics including risk assessment, offender rehabilitation, psychopathy, and youth violence. The tutorials are designed to consolidate and further develop specific topics of contemporary significance in the field.
prerequisites: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC231, PYSC241 and PSYC250

rules.description: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC231, PYSC241 and PSYC250

PSYC358.title: Applied Psychology
PSYC358.description: PSYC358 aims to introduce students to the application of psychology in non-clinical settings. The subject focuses on how psychological principles can be applied in the context of sport, health and well-being, and workplace settings. Topics covered include sport psychology, health psychology, occupational health psychology, and organisational psychology. In each topic area, students will learn how research, theory and practice are interrelated and can be applied in contemporary society.
prerequisites: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC241

rules.description: 24 credit points of 200-level PSYC subjects including PSYC241

PSYC362.title: Systems Neuroscience and Imaging
PSYC362.description: Systems Neuroscience looks at how nerve cells form a network or system that performs a task. The subject will start with the cellular, molecular, and anatomical basics of neurophysiology as required for the understanding of the following content, and will then introduce system neuroscience concepts, philosophies and principles, such as examples of computational neuroscience and explore a range of advanced computational topics and how they help understand how neuronal systems achieve their remarkable capabilities. It will also study systems such as the hippocampus or the visual system. Finally, the subject will explore modern MRI neuroimaging techniques including AI assisted uses in the study of brain systems and architectures and function at larger scales. In particular, besides lectures, the subject consists of an extensive Computer Lab/tutorial where students will analyse MRI datasets and use vibe-coding for neuroscience analysis.
prerequisites: PSYC121 AND PSYC123 OR MEDI112 AND PSYC234 OR MEDI312 OR PHYS366

rules.description: PSYC121 AND PSYC123 OR MEDI112 AND PSYC234 OR MEDI312 OR PHYS366

RESH405.title: Preliminary Research Project
RESH405.description:
This is a preliminary research project undertaken for the Bachelor of Research/Master of Research training pathway degree. The purpose of the subject is to ensure candidates will have advanced knowledge and skills for professional work or future learning. The project is undertaken under the supervision of a supervisor. The report will contain a literature review and formulate and scope the major research project to be undertaken in the second year of MRes. A seminar will be presented describing the project.
This is an independent project. It is essential that this subject be conducted in the context of regular consultation with your supervisor(s). The subject provides a scaffold, whereas supervisors will work with you on your project. Please organize times to meet with supervisors regularly.

RESH907.title: Internship
RESH907.description:
This is a  Work Integrated Learning subject for Higher Degree Research candidates undertaking an industry research internship.  In addition to the internship period, it includes CRLH900 a zero credit point subject, which focusses on Career Development Learning and employability skills.  CRLH900 equips HDR students with the skills necessary to reflect on, recognise and articulate their individual skills, values and strengths, the value of their research training and other career experiences for a range of career contexts, source relevant career opportunities, apply and plan for career experiences including Work Integrated Learning (WIL) opportunities. RESH907 fulfils the requirements of research internship schemes such as the Australian Postgraduate Research internship (APR Intern) program to maintain student enrolment during the internship period.
 
During the internship, the student works on a tightly focused research project, governed a project plan with specific deliverables.    The primary objectives of the subject are for the student to carry out a short, self-contained project (for up to 6 months) on a topic of mutual interest to the industry partner and student and in particular, for the Intern to gain relevant professional training and skills within a workplace setting relevant to their area of study.
 
The student is supported during their internship by an Academic Mentor.  The Mentor’s role is to provide guidance and support to the student undertaking the internship.  The Academic Mentor along with the student, are directly involved in the project planning stage.   Depending on the project, the Academic Mentor may directly engage with the industry partner as well as the student to achieve project outcomes, which helps develop and strengthen relationships for future engagement.
degree_restrictions: Restricted to PHD, PHD(I) students

SCII101.title: Global Challenges in Science
SCII101.description:
Every major challenge of modern life, such as ensuring energy, food, health and water security in a sustainable world has complex science and technology underpinnings that span beyond geographical barriers whilst being dependent upon often complex political and financial structures. Students in Global Challenges in Science will investigate projects related to such modern challenges in the context of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Student learning in this subject is facilitated through engaging online material, in combination with face-to-face lectures and workshop classes.
This subject will bring all students from the SMAH undergraduate science programs together in one subject. This subject will be utilised to provide course advice and guidance to help students map their program of study and navigate their transition to university. The projects undertaken in this subject will foster a sense of community amongst science students and have students explore different aspects of science and how science contributes to society.
You will explore the method of science and how science informs debate and decision-making on public issues whilst also understanding the responsibilities of the public in having scientific understanding and how you can contribute to a better future using your scientific knowledge.

SCII205.title: Introductory Geospatial Analysis
SCII205.description: This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to the theory and practice of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and geospatial analysis, and aims to equip students with core skills that will enable solving simple geospatial problems. GIS is an emergent technological platform with broad applications across natural and social sciences. It has a critical role in addressing the major challenges facing humanity, including our environmental futures; water, food, and energy security; and population heath. The subject follows a problem-based approach enabling students to apply core geo-analytical skills to solving a series of simple real-world practical problems by working both individually and in groups and using industry standard tools and technologies.

SCII213.title: Climate Change and Natural Hazards: Risks and Impacts
SCII213.description: This subject explores the complex topic of climate change and natural hazards and their impacts on human and environmental systems, including environmental and human health, infrastructure, energy, food production, water availability, and Indigenous culture and management of country. Climate change, alongside other natural hazards, represents a major challenge to physical, biological and human systems. Managing and responding to the challenges of climate change and other hazards is an expanding and critical aspect of environmental and health planning. Within this subject we will examine how the physical and chemical processes that influence Earth’s energy balance are being impacted by human activity. We investigate how the Earth regulates its climate over longer term scales and explore the carbon cycle, examining why changes in atmospheric carbon are linked to atmospheric warming. We will also examine the human behaviours that have led to climate change, such as energy production, agriculture, resource use and population. We will explore how we can respond to climate change and climate-induced changes to existing natural hazards (such as fire, flooding, drought, heat waves and coastal storms) and other natural hazards more generally. We will also examine the political and societal context of natural hazards and explore how societies plan for, respond to, and recover from disasters.

SCII311.title: Applied Geospatial Analysis
SCII311.description: This subject will provide students with the ability to develop and apply advanced geo-analytical knowledge and skills to real-world geospatial problems using a suite of spatial tools, including Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Remote Sensing. The subject follows a problem-based design and will guide students through three complex real-world geospatial problems that are applied in the local Wollongong area, in collaboration with established industry partners and collaborators in the environmental sector. Using a project lifecycle approach and working in groups, students will develop understanding of how to formulate a geospatial project from concept to solution, and how to deliver this project using industry-standard tools and technologies.

SCTI970.title: Research in Critical Social Inquiry
SCTI970.description: SCTI970 provides high-level intellectual development and support for students intending to use their research skills for a career in the public service, the non-profit sector, the tertiary education sector, or elsewhere. Strong emphasis is placed on intellectual support and the articulation of a supportive community of inquiry in the production of theses and contextual engagement in contemporary debates pertaining to students' research areas and topics.

SEA100.title: Ocean Conservation, Development and People
SEA100.description: SEA 100 introduces students to ocean conservation and development, starting with a broad introduction to activities, values and stakeholders. A recent study published in Science, analysed satellite data and determined that industrial fisheries now cover 55 per cent of the World’s oceans: an area four times larger than the terrestrial area devoted to agriculture. In addition to fisheries, our oceans provide crucial highways and oceanscapes for shipping, oil and gas, seabed mining, blue carbon, coastal development, tourism and defence all of which must balance conservation and development imperatives as they navigate and exploit our marine environment. SEA 100 leads students through a number of case studies to build knowledge of human interaction with the marine environment, critical values, ocean conservation and development challenges, and develops student expertise in critical thinking , research skills and problem solving. Guest speakers from the ANCORS network will illustrate case studies and demonstrate problem solving and engagement strategies. Lectures will be delivered online, while fortnightly workshops will engage students in analysis, problem solving and communication.

SEA300.title: Ocean Policy and Science
SEA300.description: SEA 300 introduces students to the concept of ocean policy and science. This course will provide a comprehensive overview of the link between policy and science across a wide variety of different topics. Students will learn about the transfer of science to policy, global science projects such as the UN Decade of Ocean Science, and how to conduct science fairly and equitably. Sustainable and equitable management of the oceans is key to human well-being. To achieve this, a global regulatory framework, based on science needs to be in place. SEA 300 enables students to critically think about human resources use, social problems, and science. By leading students through a diverse range of topics linked to the ocean, global politics and science, students will strengthen their research and problem-solving skills. The course will include guest lectures and panel discussions with scientists, environmental advocates, and industry stakeholders, and to build students’ understanding of the role of science in ocean policy. Lectures will be delivered online, while fortnightly workshops will engage students in analysis, problem-solving, and communication.

SEA901.title: Foundations of Ocean Law and Policy
SEA901.description: This subject will familiarise students with the important rules and concepts of public international law that underpin the Law of the Sea. It will cover the international legal system, sovereignty and jurisdiction, sources of international law, treaty making and the settlement of international disputes. It will then move on to consider the historical development of the Law of the Sea, up to and including the 1982 Law of the Sea Convention. The subject will also provide an opportunity for students to refresh key academic skills in preparation for their postgraduate studies.

SEA902.title: Law of the Sea
SEA902.description: This subject provides a comprehensive analysis of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea from a legal and policy perspective. It provides an understanding of the Convention's origins, major concepts, issues of implementation, as well as State practice.

SEA903.title: Strategy and Sea Power
SEA903.description: SEA 903 illuminates the theory and practice of sea power as an instrument of national strategy throughout history, with a particular focus upon the past two centuries. The subject considers the ideas and impact of the leading maritime strategic thinkers within their particular historical contexts, encompassing political, geostrategic, economic and military-technological factors. The continuing relevance of classical theories will be tested via their application to contemporary strategic circumstances, including the rise of China and development of modern anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) capabilities.

SEA904.title: Maritime Regulation and Enforcement
SEA904.description: This subject focuses on the specific regulatory and enforcement powers of States over different ocean activities in the various maritime zones. Key provisions of the 1982 LOSC and related international law instruments will be considered in their application to the full spectrum of maritime zones. Relevant legal and policy considerations in the development and enforcement of maritime jurisdiction will also be covered.

SEA905.title: Legal Regulation of Shipping
SEA905.description: This subject examines the regulation of shipping at the international level, particularly by analysing applicable international regulatory framework under the International Maritime Organization. It discusses key regulatory instruments for safety of navigation and the protection of the marine environment, and provides an assessment of the effectiveness of the current framework vis-à-vis the international law of the sea.

SEA906.title: Comparative Oceans Policy
SEA906.description: This subject examines the development of public policy at the national, regional and international levels to manage the oceans and their various uses, and to provide for the sustainable development and governance of ocean resources.

SEA907.title: Maritime Security Law and Policy
SEA907.description: This subject examines various maritime threats including threats against ships, ports, and offshore platforms and installations. It considers the effectiveness of international conventions addressing these threats, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (LOSC), the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code, Suppression of Unlawful Acts Against the Safety of Fixed Platforms (SUA) Convention and its Protocol, Seafarers Identity Documents (SID) Convention, and other collective and unilateral initiatives pursued after 9/11

SEA908.title: Contemporary Maritime Security Issues in the Indo-Pacific Region
SEA908.description: SEA 908 addresses the conceptualization, scope, and practice of maritime security as an important policy issue across the Indo-Pacific region. Its scope encompasses the gamut of regional maritime security problems, from conventional military competition and territorial disputes, to good order at sea issues such as disputes over navigation regimes, piracy and other law enforcement challenges, through to the relationship to energy security and the consequences of climate change impacts. The subject also assesses the role of regional cooperation in addressing maritime security problems

SEA909.title: International Marine Environmental Law
SEA909.description: This subject introduces students to the framework of international law and policy relating to environmental protection in marine areas. It aims to give students a sound understanding of key underlying concepts and principles, and covers a broad range of topics including marine pollution, biodiversity; marine protected areas; marine conservation and international trade; and climate impacts on the marine environment.

SEA910.title: Selected Topic in Maritime Studies
SEA910.description: On successful completion of this subject, students should gain a good understanding of the nominated specialised topic and be able to demonstrate superior research, analytical and writing skills. A range of topics not covered in other subjects may be offered as a Special Topic in Maritime Studies, such as climate change law and policy, marine spatial planning, marine scientific research, management of non-living resources, and region-based security studies.

SEA911.title: Research Project in Maritime Studies
SEA911.description: This subject allows students to undertake a supervised academic research project in the field of ocean law and policy. The research topic is selected upon consultation with a supervisor. The subject is assessed by a research paper of 5000 to 6000 words. This subject may be taken instead of SEA 920 capstone project

SEA912.title: Minor Thesis in Maritime Studies
SEA912.description: This subject allows students to undertake an extended supervised academic research project in the field of ocean law and policy. The research topic is selected upon consultation with a supervisor. The subject is assessed by a research paper of 10,000 to 12,000 words. This subject may be taken instead of SEA 920 capstone project

SEA913.title: The Blue Economy and Integrated Ocean Management
SEA913.description: This subject provides an introduction to the Blue Economy by examining its origins, evolution, goals, and the legal frameworks that underpin its development. Students will develop theoretical and technical knowledge of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and related areas of international law, particularly as they apply to key sectors within the Blue Economy. The course explores sector-specific approaches to managing ocean and will also introduce the concept of Integrated Ocean Management (IOM) as a way to overcome traditional sectoral boundaries and encourage collaboration among multiple stakeholders. Students will consider the environmental, economic, and socio-cultural dimensions of the Blue Economy and how they interact with IOM, including sectors such as fisheries, shipping, marine renewable energy, and coastal tourism. A strong emphasis is placed on legal and regulatory frameworks, as well as a range of tools and emerging models of integrated governance, to ensure the effective and sustainable management of ocean resources

SEA914.title: International Fisheries Law
SEA914.description: This subject examines the international and regional frameworks established to manage fisheries resources in areas under national jurisdiction and on the high seas, enforcement rights and problems, including the right of hot pursuit and bilateral and multilateral enforcement cooperation, and illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing. It analyses the role of regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs) in promoting the conservation and effective management of fisheries resources and addresses issues related to fishing by vessels of non-parties, cooperating non-parties and fishing entities.

SEA915.title: Fisheries Management
SEA915.description: This subject examines international principles for sustainable fisheries management, ecological aspects of fisheries, fisheries economics, fisheries data collection and analysis, and fisheries and coastal resource management. It looks into the application of international fisheries management principles and measures in a number of national jurisdictions. The course also discusses management frameworks established by regional fisheries organisations and the challenges confronting member States in implementing such frameworks.

SEA916.title: Fisheries and Development
SEA916.description: This subject examines the interrelationship between science, economics, the environment, trade, law and policy in the management of fisheries resources. It appraises the global nature of fisheries and fishing activities; issues related to the globalization of fisheries; and the challenges facing fisheries management and governance among states, particularly developing states. It demonstrates how important the fisheries sector can be to economic development, and links this to concepts such as human security, interdependence and the development of regional and international forms of governance of transnational fisheries issues.

SEA917.title: Integrated Monitoring, Control and Surveillance
SEA917.description: This subject explains the concept and role of MCS in supporting sustainable fisheries management. It examines the practical and operational aspects of fisheries data collection methods, licensing procedures, enforcement and prosecution. It explores the use of technology in the implementation of fisheries regulations and surveys existing regional MCS schemes. Topics covered in the subject include: the concept of MCS; licensing and authorisation to fish; record of vessels; technical and legal aspects of VMS; VMS data types and interpretation; boarding, inspection and arrest of vessels, fisheries observer programme; port State control as an MCS tool; FFA MCS strategy; IUU vessel listing; and fisheries prosecution.

SEA918.title: International Fish Trade
SEA918.description: This subject examines the international trade of fish and fish products as an important component of sustainable fisheries. It provides an extensive discussion of the interaction between international fisheries law and trade law. Examples of topics to be covered in this subject include: rules of origin; health and sanitary requirements for fish processing and trade; trade of commercially-exploited species under the Convention for the International Trade of Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES); fisheries subsidies; environmental labelling; and World Trade Organisation (WTO) fisheries and environment-related disputes.

SEA919.title: Social Dimensions of Fisheries Management and Policy
SEA919.description: This subject introduces students to the complexities associated with managing the social dimensions component of fisheries. This subject has three primary goals: 1) introduce students to social dimensions issues in fisheries (e.g. environmental impact, resource allocation, social and political conflict etc.) management and policy; 2) show students how the social dimensions of fisheries can/have been studied by a range of scientific disciplines (i.e. psychology, anthropology, sociology, communication and law); and 3) impress upon students how considering the social dimensions can benefit the management of fisheries. The subject stresses the importance of taking a multi-disciplinary approach to collaborating with the social components of fisheries, and on thinking critically, analytically and flexibly.

SEA920.title: Ocean Law and Policy Capstone
SEA920.description: The goal of the ANCORS capstone project is to allow students to meaningfully reflect on their learning in relation to law and policy for the ocean, to synthesise this learning with their broader experiences in the field and to encourage students to prepare for the next stage in their career. Students will undertake research into a current maritime issue and prepare both a written and oral report on their research. The topic is selected in consultation with a supervisor; students are encouraged to choose a topic that is of importance to their work or community. Students who wish to undertake a more traditional academic research project, including those who are considering further studies, may enrol in SEA 911 or SEA 912 instead of the SEA 920 Capstone Project.

SEA921.title: Governance of Coastal Fisheries
SEA921.description: This subject introduces students to the contemporary issues of coastal fisheries governance. This subject has three primary goals: 1) introduce students to the current worldwide issues surrounding coastal fisheries management and policy decision-making; 2) expose students to a range of disciplines which benefit sound coastal fisheries management; and 3) impress upon students how considering evidence-based learning can benefit the governance of coastal fisheries

SOC103.title: Introduction to Sociology
SOC103.description: SOC 103 Introduction to Sociology serves as an invitation to the discipline of Sociology and the study of society. The subject invites students to consider and discover: What is Sociology? How can we think sociologically? How can we use sociological perspectives to understand our social worlds? SOC103 highlights the everyday relevance of Sociology. It provides students with analytical tools to ‘see Sociology in the world’ – to make meaningful connections between the subject matter of the course and their own social worlds; and to challenge taken-for-granted assumptions and uncover underlying rules in their everyday life. Using case studies of globalisation, consumption, inequalities, families, genders, sexualities, migration, race, ethnicities, health and wellbeing, and technology, the subject introduces Sociology’s examination of the complex connections between individual behaviour and wider social forces, contexts and processes. The subject offers students the opportunity to improve communication, analytical, research, interpersonal and critical thinking skills vital for employment.

SOC104.title: Investigating Social Problems
SOC104.description: How do sociologists make sense of the world? How do they investigate social problems? The subject introduces a range of sociological methods, such as surveys, interviews, ethnography, community-based research or media analysis. But rather than simply learning about types of research, in this subject you will examine how different research methods shape what we can know about complex social issues, and why they tell vastly different stories about the same social world. You will explore how research evidence is always shaped by deeper assumptions about what counts as knowledge and how social reality can be understood. You will also learn the ethical principles underpinning research practices, and discuss how power, bias and context shape the research process. This subject provides an essential foundation in thinking about empirical research and looking at data with a “sociological eye”. It also complements SOC103, together building a strong foundation for further study in the Sociology Major and the social sciences broadly.

SOC207.title: Introduction to Social Theory
SOC207.description: This subject will provide a broad introduction to classical and contemporary debates in social theory with a specific focus on sociological themes and trends. Students will be encouraged to not only learn about key theoretical perspectives, but also to engage, analyse and critique in ways that expand the depth and rigour of sociological investigation. Students will gain an understanding of classical thinkers like Marx, Weber, and Durkheim, as well as more contemporary figures like Foucault, Butler, and Habermas in both theoretical and applied contexts. Studying social theory will challenge the way you see the world and unpack long held assumptions about power, inequality, gender and progress. As a result, the ideas contained in this subject are as useful for thinking about big picture problems and challenges as they are for developing a better understanding of everyday life. As this is an introductory subject students will be provided with the essentials necessary for pursuing further study in the area, or to enhance knowledge about key debates and ideas. This subject would be useful to all students with an interest in sociology, but it is also highly relevant for those studying politics, history, economics, cultural studies or psychology. In addition to learning about concepts in social theory, SOC207 will also develop skills in critical thinking, textual analysis, argument construction and debate.

SOC208.title: Cities, Communities and Families
SOC208.description: Cities and towns shape our personal relationships. Houses, streets, parks, and amenities all have an enormous impact on how we walk, work, drive, care for, socialise, and hook up with each other. This subject explores sociological approaches to cities, families and intimate relationships. We examine the historical transformation of cities from modern industrial metropolises to post-modern, decentralised sprawl. We look at how families are changing from heterosexual couples commuting from the suburbs into increasing numbers of single persons, single parents and blended families living without cars in inner-city, high-rise apartments. We examine changes in childhood, marriage, love, sexual identity, and dating in today’s urban ‘playground.’ We look at the increasingly diverse and multicultural nature of urban environments and families. Finally, we examine the challenges of providing affordable and social housing, connecting communities and families, integrating work and transport, and keeping cities ‘liveable’ in the face of de-industrialisation, the rise of ‘mega-cities’ and slums, and the flow and concentration of resources into fewer ‘elite’ global cities.

SOC225.title: Youth Cultures
SOC225.description: This subject addresses contemporary and historical youth cultures and subcultures, and the sociological perspectives which have been used to describe them and account for their emergence and significance. Through the media of ethnographic and documentary film, the political and social significance of youth-cultural practices is assessed. With reference to a varying range of case studies (e.g. skating, hipsters, graffiti etc.), the relationship between youth as social agents and macro structures such as the state and the market is also examined.

SOC226.title: Activism, Change and Society
SOC226.description: Activism, Change and Society explores the nature of activism and the changes it produces in society. Activism can no longer be understood to follow and be confined to traditional forms organised around class and gender. Instead, activism today emerges from a plurality of different and diverse social antagonisms based on developments around information and identity rather than dichotomies and ideologies. Examples of the new activist identities making changes to society include vegan, LGBTQI+, #MeToo, #BlackLivesMatter, fathers/men's rights etc. This subject explores these identities and more, as well as introducing students to the definitional and theoretical bases that enable a better understanding of the changing nature of activism, change and society today.

SOC227.title: Genders and Sexualities
SOC227.description: What is the difference between sex, gender and sexuality? Are there only two genders? Does femininity belong only to women? Is it true that men have the violent gene and women are born to be nurturing and gentle? Why is heterosexuality perceived as the default sexuality? Why are some sexual identities and expressions given state recognition and others criminalised? How do we make sense of the inequalities experienced by individuals and communities of non-dominant sex, gender and sexuality identities? SOC227 Genders and Sexualities explores these and other gender and sexuality related issues. Engaging with sociological perspectives such as feminist theories, queer theory and intersectionality, students will seek to understand the negotiation of diverse gender and sexual identities, expressions and practices within and across institutions such as the family, education, work, media, law, religion and healthcare. To provide a more comprehensive and inclusive learning approach, the subject will discuss different configurations of gender and sexuality across societies. The subject aims to challenge taken-for-grant assumptions about gender and sexual identities and practices so as to uncover possibilities for greater social justice and mutual respect.

SOC234.title: Social Research Methods: Practices, Problems and Politics
SOC234.description: Social research produces evidence that illuminates the social world, informs policymaking and addresses key social issues. But research is never neutral. Behind every finding lie methodological choices – choices that are shaped by and reflect social and political dynamics. Who gets counted? How are they categorised? Whose stories get told, and how? This subject asks critical questions about the role of power in social research design, practice and outcomes. Drawing on real-world qualitative and quantitative research, students will examine how exclusion and erasure operate in research design, how biased questions and the researcher’s “gaze” shape evidence, how misleading statistics carry social consequences, and how research can cause harm to the communities being studied. This subject builds critical research literacy by equipping students with skills to interrogate and evaluate social research evidence. Core to the Sociology Major and Minor, SOC234 is also highly relevant for students across disciplines in which evidence informs policy and practice, and for anyone interested in a career in research.

SOC235.title: Animals: Society, Violence, Justice
SOC235.description: Human-animal relations are wildly contradictory; some animals are protected, while others are driven to extinction; some are forcibly reproduced as ‘livestock’, while others are deemed family members. What social and cultural formations create these uneven relations?  This subject analyses human-animal relations because they are, as Levi-Strauss observed, ‘good to think with’. They illuminate taxonomies of power, stigmatisation, dehumanisation and the limitations of anthropocentric thinking. Those limitations push us to consider what justice looks like for all animals (not just the human ones)

SOC238.title: Happiness: Investigating its Causes and Conditions
SOC238.description: We will explore what is known about the causes and conditions for happiness as individuals, in interpersonal relationships and as society. The question 'how can we be happy' will be approached in an interdisciplinary fashion though various perspectives including cultural studies and cultural angles on psychology, economics and sociology. Students will develop skills and concepts for being informed, responsible independent learners who can solve problems, communicate effectively and use appropriate research methods of observation and questioning (interviews and surveys).

SOC247.title: Punishment: Purpose, Practice, Policy
SOC247.description: Retribution, deterrence, incapacitation and the maintenance of social order are some of the justifications of imprisonment. To what extent can these justifications explain the relatively high incarceration rate in Australia? How effective are theorisations like penal populism, neoliberalism, the politics of law and order and the new punitiveness, in accounting for the rise in imprisonment? The subject theorises current practices of imprisonment in Australia to develop substantiated recommendations for change.

SOC248.title: Everyday Interaction
SOC248.description: Do conversations follow unwritten 'rules'? How do we identify a joke, or an insult? What is rudeness? What resources do we draw on in producing 'normality' in mundane situations? This subject addresses everyday interaction: how we produce meaning on a day-to-day level in small-scale social settings. It introduces a range of sociological approaches to interpersonal interaction and the reproduction of the micro social order, and considers interaction in a variety of social and institutional settings.

SOC251.title: Genetics, Biotechnology and Society
SOC251.description: This subject explores the social, cultural and policy dimensions of genetics and biotechnology. It is aimed at a multidisciplinary cohort: humanities, natural science, social science and other students are welcome. They will be encouraged to reflect critically on the role of science and technology in contemporary societies and learn from past examples where technical developments went against societal needs, were rejected or were embraced with unanticipated consequences. There is a focus on learning about diverse ways of knowing, on enabling appropriate trust between biotech/genetics and society, and on what responsible research and innovation for the benefit of society might look like. Case studies may include: genetic testing and manipulation, stem cell and embryo research, genetic databases, agricultural biotechnology, or AI and nanotechnology in medicine.

SOC252.title: Revive, Resist: Belonging Amidst Difference
SOC252.description: Nearly 90% of Australians live in cities, all of which are growing in size, complexity, and cultural diversity. Most cities aspire to be the glamorous, creative, cosmopolitan, ‘global cities’ of tomorrow. However, they are also paying the price of upheaval and fragmentation, creating challenges for social justice and equity that come with fully engaging with the global economy. An area like Western Sydney, for example, is seen as both a hub of new enterprise, youthful sporting achievement, and enviable culinary diversity, but also as a space with ongoing challenges posed by belonging and socio-economic disadvantage. In many cities, such issues play out against a backdrop of increasingly unaffordable housing, urban sprawl, poor transport options, and communities gated and segregated by ethnicity and visa status. This subject will explore the intersection between globalised economies, skilled and refugee migration, multiculturalism, and urban development and change. Taking a transnational and intersectional approach, it will look closely at how issues of race, gender, environment, and class combine to influence patterns of segregation and economic division, but also where bridges of cosmopolitan openness are being built.

SOC280.title: Work Cultures
SOC280.description: This subject is about work and workplace cultures. It is core to the Work Cultures minor currently underdevelopment. The subject aims to explicitly prepare students for the world of work by (a) introducing them to a range of literature on workplace organisation, interaction, and culture, such as to sensitise them to tacit features of and expectations in work environments, and (b) setting them to conduct research on features of the actual labour markets they are in now and/or into which they will enter upon graduation.

SOC328.title: Doing Sociology - Sociology Capstone
SOC328.description: SOC328 is the capstone subject for the Sociology Major. As such it brings all completing SOC Major students together into a final core subject group. It offers students the opportunity to draw on the sociological knowledge they have acquired throughout their major and bring it to the development of an applied sociological research project. It also encourages students to reflect on potential career paths and the role of sociology in the workplace and the broader world. The applied focus of the research project enables students to explore how their sociological knowledge and research have practical applications and provide possibilities for improving outcomes for different groups of people. The subject and the project enable students to identify and integrate recognised professional skills into their project. These include (as defined by The Australian Sociological Association): understanding social and cultural issues; high quality communication skills; research and detailed observation; and the ability to work independently.
prerequisites: 6cp of 100 level SOC and SOC 207 and SOC 234 and 6cp of 200 or 300 level SOC.
