rules.description: 6cp of 100 level SOC and SOC 207 and SOC 234 and 6cp of 200 or 300 level SOC.

SOC329.title: Globalisation and Social Transformation
SOC329.description: This subject explores social and cultural change in Australia and across other world regions through the context of globalization. The subject discusses theories of social and cultural change, and draws on a range of case studies to illustrate the increasingly interconnected nature of the contemporary world. It considers the historical legacies of colonialism and post-WW2 development, and the ways in which historical and contemporary global forces shape the world we live in. Topics addressed may include: media and cultural flows; migration; new social movements; changing sex and gender identities; changing patterns of work and leisure; and precarity, poverty, and inequality.

SOC344.title: Emotions, Bodies & Society
SOC344.description: This subject will explore how different emotions are constructed, experienced, disciplined, and otherwise worked at and managed across a variety of public and private social circumstances, and within human bodies. It will review the historical duality of mind and body, the civilising/disciplining process, and the rise of complex emotions in modern society. It will explore gendered emotions and the concept of emotion management. It will also explore a range of different emotions in social contexts. These include emotions associated with social status (anger and shame); with prosperity, wealth and health (joy and happiness); with consumption, attraction and repulsion (admiration, jealousy and envy); with cyborg theory and body modification (excitement, satisfaction); with disability and stigma (fear, anxiety, shame), and with isolation in late modernity (sadness, depression, loneliness).

SOC347.title: Sociology of Health, Illness and Medicine
SOC347.description: Why do fitness apps make us feel guilty? Why do some patients get listened to and not others? Is ADHD a medical condition or a social category? SOC347 takes the tools of sociology and science and technology studies (STS) and turns them on medicine, an institution at the centre of our lives.Over the first part of semester, you will encounter six analytical lenses and see them applied to cases including reproductive medicine, patient activism, and wearable technologies. You will learn to ask uncomfortable but productive questions: who decides what counts as healthy, sick, or at risk? What roles do technologies, pharmaceutical companies, governments and patients themselves play in shaping medicine? How does medicine changes bodies and identities, and to whose benefits?In the last part of semester, you will choose a contemporary case study that interests you and conduct your own original analysis using the lens that fits best. Past students have explored AI diagnostics, mental health apps, precision medicine and disability technologies among many others.No prior sociology is required. The subject is designed to be intellectually rewarding whether you come from sociology, nutrition, cell biology, medical biotechnology, or anywhere else. You'll complete the subject with a toolkit for thinking critically about health, science and technology that applies well beyond the classroom.

SOC348.title: Race, Migration and Diversity
SOC348.description: Black Lives Matter, Covid-related racism, Indigenous rights movements and immigrant detention are just some of the current social phenomena this subject on race, migration and diversity will cover. SOC351 provides a sociological examination of the power structure of race, and how the persistent subjugation and resulting precarity of racialised, colonised and marginalised populations continue till today. Using sociological perspectives, we will explore different forms of racism and violence by considering existing systems, social problems and real life situations in local and global contexts. Closely related to the structure of race is border control and migration regimes. Both topics hinge upon these crucial questions on humanity: Whose lives matter more? What is the hierarchy of value of human lives? How does this hierarchy manifest in social relations and state policies? How do interconnected systems of domination like racism and xenophobia keep this hierarchy in place? The subject invites students to employ an intersectional perspective to carefully consider these pertinent questions on power, precarity and inequalities along the lines of race, class, nationality, ethnicity, gender and sexuality. With the proliferation of diversity and inclusion programs across sectors and industries, students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of these diversity corporate initiatives to address inequalities and injustices. Lastly, the subject encourages students to reimagine more equal and just futures for those less supported by systems.

SOC352.title: Power, Resistance and Society
SOC352.description: SOC352 Power, Resistance and Society has a focus on ‘political sociology’. This subject will specifically explore the foundational concepts and theories within the field including some contemporary challenges to political society or state power and sovereignty as well as, challenges to civil society and in particular the people and popular consciousness.

SOC356.title: Cultures of Dispossession
SOC356.description: SOC356 Cultures of Dispossession explores the emergence and implications of economic and political integration and rationalisation. It investigates the internal logic and social consequences of dominant forms of governance and organisation, such as bureaucratic administration and the monetisation of social and material exchange. Through a range of case studies, the subject addresses topics such as concentration of wealth and the nature of finance capital, the economic origins and implications of climate change, and the management of state borders. The subject also explores movements, perspectives and practices that critique and counter these structural problems, such as mutual aid, just transition, and food sovereignty.

SOWK234.title: Welfare State and Human Services
SOWK234.description: This subject provides students with an introduction to the Australian welfare state and the contemporary human services system. Contemporary debates on the nature of the welfare state will be explored, in particular, the neo-liberal challenge and the restructuring as a result of increasing diversity, technological disruption and globalisation. It also introduces students to the role of social workers in human services organisations, and service delivery and management will be explored. Students will develop beginning skills in organisational analysis.

SPAN151.title: Spanish for Beginners 1
SPAN151.description: This subject for beginners or near beginners in Spanish presupposes no prior knowledge of the language. SPAN151 students will develop communication skills for common situations. Students will learn Spanish vocabulary and grammar in everyday contexts (e.g. family, classes, hobbies, sports and travel) to develop proficiency in listening, speaking, reading and writing. There is an emphasis on the communicative functions and the development of those skills necessary to achieve a basic understanding of the Spanish language.

SPAN152.title: Spanish for Beginners 2
SPAN152.description: This subject builds on and consolidates the content from SPAN151.Students further develop their proficiency in listening, speaking, reading and writing, emphasising communicative and structural aspects of the language. Students start understanding and expressing more nuanced meaning, such as describing events in the past.

SPAN241.title: Intermediate Spanish 1
SPAN241.description: This subject builds on and consolidates the content from SPAN152. Listening, speaking, reading and writing are practised throughout SPAN241 but this subject places a higher emphasis on listening and on communicative skills. Students learn more complex structures of the language to express opinions and defend their point of view.
prerequisites: SPAN152 or equivalent.  (Students who have not completed SPAN152 but have completed an equivalent subject need the approval of the subject coordinator to enrol)

rules.description: SPAN152 or equivalent.  (Students who have not completed SPAN152 but have completed an equivalent subject need the approval of the subject coordinator to enrol)

SPAN242.title: Intermediate Spanish 2
SPAN242.description: SPAN242 focuses on using acquired language structures and vocabulary to analyse and discuss short films and literary texts. The grammar learned in previous SPAN subjects is consolidated and extended. A greater emphasis is placed on speaking and writing skills.

STAT101.title: Introduction to Statistics
STAT101.description:
This subject introduces students to essential statistical tools and concepts for understanding, analysing and communicating variation and uncertainty in real-world contexts. Students will learn how to display and summarise univariate data, explore relationships in bivariate data, and interpret association, correlation and simple linear regression.
The subject also provides an introduction to probability theory, including Bayes’ rule and the law of total probability, as well as random variables and key discrete and continuous probability distributions, including the binomial, geometric, uniform and Normal distributions. Students will further develop an understanding of sampling distributions, confidence intervals for a population mean, and the basic principles of hypothesis testing.
Throughout the subject, students will use appropriate statistical computing software to analyse data and interpret results. The subject also emphasises the development of clear statistical communication skills in both written and oral forms.

STAT201.title: Random Variables and Estimation
STAT201.description: STAT201 is the second statistics subject following STAT101. It provides the theoretical foundation (introductory probability theory) for more advanced statistics subjects which rely on this theory. It builds on STAT101 and introduces new discrete random variables (Poisson distribution, Hypergeometric, Uniform) and new continuous random variables (Exponential and Gamma distributions, Uniform, Beta and Cauchy), and teaches concepts such as expected values; transformations; moment generating functions; mutlivariate distributions; the Law of large numbers; and the Central Limit Theorem. STAT201 also introduces the major estimation and hypothesis testing concepts and many common analysis techniques. Topics include inference techniques, which include sampling distributions (such as the chi-squared, t and F distributions), methods and criteria of estimation. and hypothesis testing and investigates the relationship between Size, Power and sample size. Students will learn a popular freely available statistical software package that has become increasingly important in recent years in academia, and in the job market.
prerequisites: ((MATH188 or MATH110 or MATH142) and (STAT101 or STAT131)) or MATH283

rules.description: ((MATH188 or MATH110 or MATH142) and (STAT101 or STAT131)) or MATH283

STAT250.title: Managing and Communicating Data
STAT250.description:
A crucial skill in data science is the management and organisation of data. Usually, the most time-consuming step in analyses is the setup and shaping of data for the required analyses.
Visualisation of data, whether used for exploratory analysis or for illustration of results, is a must in any translational project and for collaboration between and within disciplines. The capability of updating analyses, for example, when new data become available, is becoming a necessary skill.
This subject will cover data wrangling, which involves reading in data sets from different sources, cleaning data, and aggregating and summarising variables and rows from data. It will also cover basics of administrative data use and existence of resources for accessing data.  This subject will rely heavily on statistical packages such as R, RStudio and RMarkdown.

STAT251.title: Fundamentals of Biostatistics
STAT251.description: STAT251 enables students to understand the statistical content of articles in their own discipline. Includes exploratory data analysis; samples and populations; elementary probability; the Normal, binomial and Poisson distributions; estimation and confidence intervals; hypothesis testing for means, proportions and regression analysis; sensitivity and specificity.

STAT252.title: Statistics For the Natural Sciences
STAT252.description: STAT252 provides an introduction to statistical techniques. Topics covered are: data presentation; probability, binomial and Poisson distributions; Normal distribution; inference for single samples; comparison of two samples; analysis of variance and multiple comparisons; linear regression and correlation; goodness-of-fit testing and contingency tables.

STAT332.title: Generalised Linear Models
STAT332.description: This unit considers how to investigate relationships between variables arising from observational studies and designed experiments. Topics include: Model fitting as an approach to statistical analysis, Exponential family of distributions, Maximum likelihood estimation, Inference methods based on model fitting, Models for multiple linear regression; estimation and analysis; diagnostics and model selection. Generalised linear models for categorical data; logistic regression for nominal and ordinal data, Poisson regression and log-linear models and Additive models

STAT351.title: Fundamentals of Data Science and Machine Learning
STAT351.description: STAT351 is an introduction to machine learning concepts and methods that are relevant to a variety of fields. The subject demonstrates how data science and machine learning integrate perspectives of statistics, computer science, and domain-expertise. Students will gain a broad understanding of how to implement, interpret, and make decisions informed by common supervised and unsupervised methods such as linear and logistic regression, classification and regression trees, neural networks, support vector machines, principal component analysis and clustering. The subject will be taught with R and RStudio, though students are not expected to have previous experience with the R statistical programming language. Note: Students who have completed INFO411 prior to studying STAT351 will not receive credit for STAT351. Students who complete STAT351 first may continue on to complete INFO411 and receive credit for both.

STAT950.title: Managing and Communicating Health and Social Data
STAT950.description:
A crucial skill in data science is the management and organisation of data. Usually, the most time-consuming step in analyses is the setup and shaping of data for the required analyses. 
Visualisation of data, whether used for exploratory analysis or for illustration of results, is a must in any translational project and for collaboration between and within disciplines. The capability of updating analyses, for example, when new data become available, or to share research and analyses, so others can reproduce the results is becoming a necessary step in presenting/publishing research. 
This subject will cover basics of reproducibility of research. The documenting of code scripts, dynamic document and analysis creation, and analysis/coding good practices will be covered. The subject will rely heavily on statistical packages such as R, RStudio and RMarkdown. 
The subject will cover data wrangling, which involves reading in data sets from different sources, cleaning data, and aggregating and summarising variables and rows from data. This subject will also cover basics of administrative data use and existence of resources for accessing data.

STAT951.title: Data Science and Machine Learning for Health and Social Sciences
STAT951.description: Data science and machine learning sit at the intersection of statistics, computer science and domain expertise and are becoming increasingly integral to research and evidence-based decision making in health and social sciences. However, these methods are not a panacea and require careful implementation.STAT951 provides an introductory foundation to machine learning concepts and methods applied to health and social data. Students will gain a broad understanding of how to implement, interpret, and make decisions informed by common supervised and unsupervised methods. These techniques include linear and logistic regression, classification and regression trees, neural networks, support vector machines, principal component analysis and clustering. The subject will be taught with R and RStudio. Students are not expected to have previous experience with the R statistical programming language, but they are encouraged to complete STAT950 (or similar) prior to commencing STAT951.

STS112.title: Changing Perceptions of Nature
STS112.description: This subject introduces students to the ways in which perceptions of nature fundamentally changed during the modern era. It focuses on two major shifts in attitudes and beliefs: the Scientific Revolution between the 16th and 18th centuries, and the Darwinian Revolution between the late 18th and 20th centuries. The first revolution involved a movement away from perceptions of nature as an organic, living thing  which could be explained by contemplating and classifying its features, to thinking of nature as a machine which could be pulled apart experimentally and understood mathematically. The second revolution involved a shift from creationist theories of the origins of life and the cosmos to the development of evolutionary explanations that did not involve divine intervention. These new conceptions of nature were shaped by broader cultural, political and economic factors such as religious beliefs, humanism, warfare, exploration and colonization, the emergence of capitalism, and new technologies and industry.

UOW200.title: Innovation and Impact in Practice
UOW200.description: This subject equips students with transdisciplinary problem-solving skills by tackling a complex organisational issue provided by a partner organisation. By integrating different perspectives, data, information, tools, concepts, techniques and theories from multiple disciplines, students will discover new and impactful ways to tackle organisational problems together. Students will develop innovative and entrepreneurial solutions that take the systemic and context-specific nature of the problem into consideration. Students present their analysis and impactful innovative solution to the sponsoring organisation and a panel of experts who provide feedback and input. The subject integrates innovation and entrepreneurial learning modules developed by is UOW’s iAccelerate and is delivered in partnership with UOW’s award winning accelerator program.

UOW300.title: Entrepreneurship for Impact
UOW300.description: This subject equips students with tools, techniques and thought processes necessary to start their own entrepreneurial journey with the support of industry professionals. Students evaluate innovative opportunities from a range of perspectives and disciplines including financial, technical/ engineering, and legal in order to identify a feasible and authentic idea for an impactful start-up. Students conduct market research on their opportunity, develop a plan for exploitation and have the opportunity to present their proposal to a panel of experts who provide feedback on the commercial feasibility of the chosen project and how to strengthen overall impact. The subject integrates innovative and entrepreneurial learning content/ modules developed by is UOW’s iAccelerate and is delivered in partnership with UOW’s award winning accelerator program.
prerequisites: UOW 200 or CRLP200 or a minimum of 96 credit points

rules.description: UOW 200 or CRLP200 or a minimum of 96 credit points

CSCI318.title: Software Engineering Practices & Principles
CSCI318.description: This subject examines the current state of software engineering both as an academic discipline and as a profession. The subject focuses on issues of requirements engineering, system procurement, and professional practice, and through case studies, the subject considers reasons for the failure and success of various software engineering projects. Topics include: Requirements Elicitation, Functional and Non-Functional Requirements, Design Patterns and Refactoring, Reverse Engineering, Software Quality Assurance, Analysis and Verification of Specification and Design, Examples of Formal Techniques in Software Engineering.

CSCI322.title: Systems Administration
CSCI322.description: This subject offers a comprehensive examination of systems administration. Students will develop the practical skills and theoretical knowledge to effectively design, deploy, and manage network infrastructures and servers. The curriculum covers configuring essential network services, implementing data management technologies, and securing systems against various threats. Emphasising professional practices and analytical skills, the subject prepares students for systems administration roles adaptable to any platform.
prerequisites: CSIT127 plus 18 credit points at 200 level

rules.description: CSIT127 plus 18 credit points at 200 level

CSCI388.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
CSCI388.description: This subject explores concepts and principles underlying virtual reality and augmented reality applications for various platforms. The subject will introduce students to theories and techniques required to gain an understanding of virtual and augmented reality technologies, which will allow students to devise solutions for these interactive technologies. The subject will also provide students with practical hands-on experience in designing and developing virtual and augmented reality applications using appropriate hardware and software.
prerequisites: CSIT121 and 18 credit points at 200 level

rules.description: CSIT121 and 18 credit points at 200 level

CSIT205.title: Generative AI
CSIT205.description: In this subject, students delve into the world of Generative AI. They explore the foundational principles and practical applications of this cutting-edge field. Through a blend of theory and hands-on experience, students gain insights into how Generative AI empowers artificial intelligence to create original content - ranging from text and images to video and code - based on user prompts. The curriculum covers essential topics, including AI’s role in code generation, effective prompt engineering techniques, and the development of advanced generative models like GANs and transformers. Moreover, students critically examine the ethical implications of Generative AI and its impact on business strategy. By the end of the subject, students will have a comprehensive understanding of this promising field and the ability to responsibly apply Generative AI in real-world scenarios.

CSIT305.title: Emerging Information Technologies and their Applications
CSIT305.description: This subject introduces students to emerging information technologies and their practical applications. Students will have a deep understanding of innovative technologies such as specialised processors, while also delving into modern software development practices (e.g., Agile and DevOps methodologies). It covers advanced networking technologies (e.g., 5G and IoT architectures) and examines contemporary data management and storage solutions (e.g., data warehousing and data lakes), emphasizing security, privacy, and big data applications. This subject will equip students with advanced knowledge of emerging information technologies and enhance their skills to appropriately choose and apply information techniques to resolve practical problems effectively.

CSIT328.title: Web Security
CSIT328.description: The web, also known as World Wide Web (WWW), is now one of the essential Internet services. However, as web services become versatile, the number of web vulnerabilities has increased dramatically. In this subject, students will gain insight into the latest web threats. They will also learn the fundamentals of web security and understand the technical aspects of web defence.

CSIT377.title: Enterprise Cloud Development
CSIT377.description: Cloud Computing is the on-demand delivery of computational resources like hardware infrastructure, applications, servers, storage, databases, networking, and software over the Internet. This subject aims to provide fundamental knowledge and applicable hands-on skills for enterprise-level Cloud Computing. The subject covers various cloud deployment models (public, private, hybrid) and service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, serverless), enabling a critical understanding of how different cloud solutions are structured and delivered. Students are exposed to ready-to-implement solutions for enterprise IT systems through common cloud computing technologies that enable microservice architecture, Web APIs, mashup software, and similar applications. The subject provides hands-on experience in designing and developing scalable, reliable, and secure cloud solutions using a mainstream cloud computing platform.
prerequisites: CSIT128 and 6 credit points at 200 level

MATH221.title: Mathematics for Computer Science
MATH221.description: MATH221 delivers core skills required for learning in computer science. Such skills include logic, formal proof, formal data structures and relations between these data structures. Realised mathematically as sets, bijections, equivalence classes, and graphs, MATH221 gives students hands-on experience with basic mathematical manipulations of these structures, as well as an exposition on their most fundamental properties.

ACCY112.title: Accounting In Organisations
ACCY112.description: The subject advances understanding of accounting in organisations. The subject introduces accounting for complex equity structures, and develops the theoretical and technical aspects of accounting for assets and the protection of assets through internal controls. Accounting for the past and future is examined through the introduction of cost structures and their application in solving fundamental business problems using cost-volume profit analysis. The application of budgets is explored.

ECON251.title: Industry and Trade in Asia
ECON251.description: This subject studies the neo-classical, structuralist and culturalists views on industrialisation in Asia using country specific examples. It examines and applies trade and industry policy, economic integration, investment flows and the international monetary system. It further explores the East Asian Model and its application by other countries in the region. The causes of extraordinary growth and meltdown in Asian countries are analysed. The recent challenges in the region and the strategies to overcome the main challenges are emphasised.

MATH223.title: Mathematics for Information Technology
MATH223.description: MATH223 is a core subject for information technology students, providing key mathematical and statistical knowledge. The subject is split into two strands: the Calculus Strand and the Data Analysis Strand. Calculus Strand: This strand begins by reviewing mathematical principles and tools that support analysis in the IT workplace, including algebraic concepts, summation, polynomials, integrals, derivatives, and special functions (exp, log). The material is applied to understand essential concepts in mathematical finance. The strand concludes with project evaluation techniques, such as return-on-investment. Data Analysis Strand: This strand applies the core mathematical concepts to discrete and continuous probability. The strand begins with basic data analysis, including univariate and bivariate data, association, correlation and simple linear regression. Study continues with discrete probability models (binomial and Poisson) and continuous distributions, including normal and uniform. The subject ends with confidence intervals and introductory hypothesis testing, such as the Chi-squared test for association and one-sample t-test.
